<a id="62-index-structures"></a>
### 6.2 Index Structures

This subchapter explains how each of PostgreSQL's built-in index types is organized, which operators it can accelerate, and what it costs, ending with a guide for choosing between them. All index types share one design: an index is a separate structure whose entries point to heap tuples by `ctid`, and the table itself stays a heap.

#### B-Tree Indexes

Without an index, the only way to find the events of user 4242 is a **sequential scan**: read all 11,000-plus pages of `events` and test every row. That is fine for a report that needs most rows, and hopeless for a web page that needs ten. A book solves the same problem with an index at the back: sorted terms with page numbers, so you jump to the right page instead of reading the whole book. A **B-tree** ("balanced tree") index is that idea built for a disk: sorted keys, each with the `ctid` of its row, organized so that any key can be found by reading only a handful of pages.

**Structure.** A B-tree is a tree of 8 KB pages:

- **Leaf pages** hold the index entries, `(key, ctid)`, sorted by key. Each leaf is linked to its left and right neighbors, so a range can be read by walking sideways.
- **Internal pages** hold separator keys and pointers to child pages. They exist only to guide the search.
- The **root** is the single page at the top. All leaves are at the same depth, which is what "balanced" means.

```text
                               [ root:  < 40000 | >= 40000 ]
                              /                               \
           [ internal: <15000 | <28000 | ... ]        [ internal: <52000 | ... ]
            /           |            \                         ...
   [leaf: 1..412] <-> [leaf: 413..824] <-> ... <-> [leaf: 99600..100000]
     (key, ctid)        (4242, (88,17))
                        (4242, (403,2))       sorted entries; neighbors linked for range scans
                        (4242, (9021,55))
```

Because each internal page holds hundreds of separators, the tree is very shallow. With about 400 entries per page, three levels reach 64 million keys and four levels reach 25 billion. A lookup reads one page per level, and the upper levels are almost always cached in memory.

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_user_id_idx ON events (user_id);

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;
SELECT level FROM bt_metap('events_pkey');
--  level
-- -------
--      2         -- root is 2 levels above the leaves: any id is found in 3 page reads
```

**Before and after.** `EXPLAIN` shows how the planner reads the table ([7.3](#73-reading-execution-plans)):

```sql
-- Before the index existed:
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 4242;
--  Gather
--    Workers Planned: 2
--    ->  Parallel Seq Scan on events          -- every page read, every row tested
--          Filter: (user_id = 4242)

-- After CREATE INDEX:
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 4242;
--  Bitmap Heap Scan on events
--    Recheck Cond: (user_id = 4242)
--    ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_user_id_idx    -- tree descent, ~10 matching ctids
--          Index Cond: (user_id = 4242)
```

With `\timing` in psql, the query drops from tens of milliseconds to well under one.

**What a B-tree can answer.** Because entries are sorted, a B-tree supports every question about order, for any type with a sort order (numbers, text, dates, UUIDs, ...):

| Query shape | Example |
|---|---|
| Equality | `WHERE id = 42`, `WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3)` |
| Ranges | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `BETWEEN` |
| `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` | `WHERE shipped_at IS NULL` |
| Prefix match | `WHERE sku LIKE 'LAP%'` (with the `C` collation or `text_pattern_ops`) |
| Sorted output | `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10`: no sort step, the index is read in order |
| `min()` / `max()` | Read one end of the index |

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_created_at_idx ON events (created_at);

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;
--  Limit
--    ->  Index Scan Backward using events_created_at_idx on events   -- leaves walked right to left
```

Index entries can be declared `DESC` and `NULLS FIRST`/`NULLS LAST`. A single-column index can be read in either direction, so this matters only for multicolumn indexes with mixed directions ([Column Order in Composite Indexes](#column-order-in-composite-indexes)).

**Three ways to use an index.** The plan node shows how the matching rows are fetched:

| Node | How it works | Chosen when |
|---|---|---|
| Index Scan | Walk the index, fetch each row from the heap in index order | Few rows, or output must be in index order |
| Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan | Collect all matching `ctid`s into a bitmap, sort by page, then read each heap page once | Moderate numbers of rows scattered over the table |
| Index Only Scan | Answer from the index alone, skipping the heap for all-visible pages | All needed columns are in the index ([Index-Only Scans](#index-only-scans)) |

**Space-saving features.** Since PostgreSQL 13, B-trees **deduplicate** equal keys into one entry with a list of `ctid`s, which makes indexes on columns with many repeated values (`user_id`, `status`) much smaller. Since 14, **bottom-up deletion** removes obsolete entries from a page before splitting it, which slows index growth on update-heavy tables.

**Limits.** An entry must fit in about a third of a page (2,704 bytes on a standard build). Indexing very long text values with a B-tree fails with an error for oversized rows; use a hash index or an index on `md5(column)` for equality on such values.

The B-tree is the default (`CREATE INDEX` without `USING`), the only index type that can enforce uniqueness, and the right choice for the large majority of indexes.

**Key takeaways**

- A B-tree stores sorted `(key, ctid)` entries in linked leaf pages under a shallow tree of internal pages; lookups read 3-4 pages even for billions of rows.
- It supports equality, ranges, `IS NULL`, prefix `LIKE`, sorted output, and `min`/`max` for any sortable type.
- The planner reads it with an Index Scan, a Bitmap scan, or an Index Only Scan, depending on how many rows match.
- It is the default index type and the only one that supports `UNIQUE`.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `EXPLAIN` for `SELECT * FROM events WHERE id BETWEEN 100 AND 200` and for `... WHERE id > 100` and explain why the plans differ.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Use `bt_metap` and `bt_page_stats` (from `pageinspect`) to find the depth of `events_user_id_idx` and the number of entries on its root page. Estimate how many leaf pages it has and check against `pg_relation_size`.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why does PostgreSQL use B-trees rather than binary search trees or hash tables as its default index?" *Hint:* Think about the cost of each page read, how many keys fit on one page, range queries, and sorted output.

#### Hash Indexes

A B-tree compares whole keys at every level and stores the full key in every entry. For a column of long values that is only ever searched with `=`, such as URLs, tokens, or file paths, that is wasted work: there is no need to know which URL comes "before" another. A **hash index** stores only a 4-byte hash code of each key and finds matches by jumping straight to the right bucket, like a coat check that gives you a numbered ticket instead of a description of your coat.

**Structure**

```text
 key 'https://shop.example/p/ultrabook-14?ref=mail'
        |
     hash() -> 0x9F3A21C7 -> bucket 7
        |
 [meta page] -> [bucket 0] [bucket 1] ... [bucket 7] -> [overflow page] -> ...
                                          (hash, ctid) entries, sorted by hash code
```

A lookup computes the hash, reads the bucket's pages, and fetches the matching rows from the heap, where the actual value is rechecked (different keys can share a hash code). The number of buckets doubles gradually as the table grows.

**Usage**

```sql
CREATE TABLE visits (
  id  bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  url text NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO visits (url)
SELECT 'https://shop.example/products/' || md5(g::text) || '?utm_source=newsletter'
FROM generate_series(1, 1000000) AS g;                     -- ~85-character URLs

CREATE INDEX visits_url_btree ON visits (url);
CREATE INDEX visits_url_hash  ON visits USING hash (url);

SELECT indexrelname, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid))
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE relname = 'visits';
-- visits_url_btree  ~ 100 MB     (stores every 85-byte key)
-- visits_url_hash   ~ 30-40 MB   (stores 4-byte hash codes; sizes vary)

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT id FROM visits WHERE url = 'https://shop.example/products/c4ca4238a0b923820dcc509a6f75849b?utm_source=newsletter';
--  Index Scan using visits_url_hash on visits
--    Index Cond: (url = '...'::text)
```

**Hash versus B-tree**

| | Hash | B-tree |
|---|---|---|
| Operators | `=` only | `=`, ranges, prefix `LIKE`, sorting |
| Entry size | Fixed (hash code + `ctid`), whatever the key length | Grows with key length |
| Unique indexes | No | Yes |
| Multicolumn | No | Yes |
| Index-only scans | No (the value itself is not stored) | Yes |
| Crash-safe and replicated | Yes, since PostgreSQL 10 | Yes |

Before version 10, hash indexes were not written to the WAL, were not crash-safe, and were not replicated, which is why older guides warn against them. That advice is outdated, but B-trees with deduplication are still competitive in most cases. Choose hash when keys are long, queries use only equality, and benchmarks on your data show a real gain.

**Key takeaways**

- A hash index maps each key's 32-bit hash code to a bucket and supports only `=`.
- Its entries have a fixed size, so it can be much smaller than a B-tree on long keys.
- It cannot enforce uniqueness, span several columns, provide ordering, or serve index-only scans.
- It is safe to use since PostgreSQL 10; prefer it only for equality lookups on long values.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create both index types on `visits.url`, run an equality query and a `LIKE 'https://shop.example/products/a%'` query, and check which index each one uses.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Measure the size of a B-tree and a hash index on a `text` column with 10-character values and again with 200-character values. At which length does the hash index start to win on size?
> 3. **(Interview)** "Hash tables have O(1) lookup and B-trees have O(log n). Why is the B-tree still the default?" *Hint:* Count actual page reads for each with realistic fan-out, then list the query types each one supports.

#### GiST Indexes

A B-tree needs keys that can be put in a single sorted line. Many data types have no such order. Which comes first, a circle in Paris or a polygon around Berlin? Is the range 9:00-11:00 "less than" 10:00-12:00? The useful questions for such data are different: *does it overlap*, *is it contained in*, *what is nearest to*. **GiST** (Generalized Search Tree) is a framework for balanced trees that answer these questions. Instead of separator keys, each internal entry holds a **summary predicate** that covers everything below it, such as a bounding box around all shapes in a subtree.

**Structure (as an R-tree for 2-D data)**

```text
 +----------------------------- root ------------------------------+
 |  +------ A ------+                   +--------- B ----------+    |
 |  | . p1          |                   |        . p4          |    |
 |  |      . p2     |    query box      |   . p5        . p6   |    |
 |  |   . p3     +==|=========+         +----------------------+    |
 |  +------------|--+         |                                     |
 |               +============+                                     |
 +------------------------------------------------------------------+

 root entries: [box A -> page A] [box B -> page B]
 Search "points inside the query box": box A overlaps it -> descend; box B does not -> skip
```

Unlike B-tree key ranges, the boxes of sibling entries may **overlap**, so a search may need to descend into several branches. Summaries can also be **lossy** (a bounding box is larger than the shapes inside it), so candidates are rechecked against the real value.

**What GiST indexes in core PostgreSQL**

| Data | Typical operators | Example question |
|---|---|---|
| Geometric types (`point`, `box`, `polygon`, `circle`) | `&&` overlaps, `@>` contains, `<->` distance | Stores within a map area |
| Range and multirange types | `&&`, `@>`, `<@`, `-|-` adjacent | Bookings that overlap a period |
| `inet` / `cidr` (with `inet_ops`) | `<<`, `>>=`, `&&` | Which network contains an IP |
| `tsvector` | `@@` | Full-text search (lossy; GIN is usually better, [5.3](#53-full-text-search)) |
| Extensions: PostGIS, `pg_trgm`, `btree_gist`, `ltree`, `cube` | Various | Geography, fuzzy text, hierarchies |

**Overlap queries on ranges.** The classic use is preventing or finding overlapping periods. An exclusion constraint ([Exclusion Constraints](#exclusion-constraints)) is itself enforced by a GiST index:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;          -- lets GiST handle "room_id WITH =" too

CREATE TABLE room_bookings (
  id      bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  room_id int       NOT NULL,
  during  tstzrange NOT NULL,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)   -- creates a GiST index on (room_id, during)
);

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM room_bookings
WHERE room_id = 12 AND during && tstzrange('2025-06-01 09:00+00', '2025-06-01 12:00+00');
--  Index Scan using room_bookings_room_id_during_excl on room_bookings
--    Index Cond: ((room_id = 12) AND (during && '["2025-06-01 09:00:00+00","2025-06-01 12:00:00+00")'::tstzrange))
```

**Nearest-neighbor search.** GiST can return rows in order of distance, reading only as much of the tree as needed. This "KNN" search uses the distance operator `<->` in `ORDER BY`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE stores (
  id       int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name     text  NOT NULL,
  location point NOT NULL                          -- (longitude, latitude), simplified
);
INSERT INTO stores (name, location)
SELECT 'Store ' || g, point(-10 + random() * 40, 35 + random() * 25)   -- scattered over Europe
FROM generate_series(1, 100000) AS g;

CREATE INDEX stores_location_gist ON stores USING gist (location);

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT name FROM stores ORDER BY location <-> point '(2.35, 48.85)' LIMIT 5;   -- 5 closest to Paris
--  Limit
--    ->  Index Scan using stores_location_gist on stores
--          Order By: (location <-> '(2.35,48.85)'::point)     -- no sort: the index yields nearest first
```

**Costs.** GiST indexes are slower to build and usually slower to search than a B-tree for data a B-tree can handle, because of overlapping subtrees and rechecks. Their value is that they make whole classes of queries indexable at all.

**Key takeaways**

- GiST is a framework for balanced trees whose internal entries are summaries (such as bounding boxes) covering their subtrees.
- It answers overlap, containment, and nearest-neighbor questions for geometric, range, network, and extension types.
- Subtrees can overlap and summaries can be lossy, so searches may visit several branches and recheck rows.
- Exclusion constraints and KNN `ORDER BY ... <-> ... LIMIT n` queries are its signature uses.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** With the `stores` table, find all stores inside the box `box '((2,48),(3,49))'` using `location <@ box`, with and without the GiST index, and compare the plans.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Insert 100,000 random bookings into `room_bookings` (skipping conflicts with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`) and write a query listing, for one room, all free one-hour slots on a given day. Check that it uses the index.
> 3. **(Interview)** "How would you find the 10 restaurants nearest to a user, among 5 million, in a few milliseconds?" *Hint:* Consider what a plain `ORDER BY distance LIMIT 10` costs without an index, how KNN search in GiST avoids sorting, and what PostGIS adds over the built-in `point` type.

#### SP-GiST Indexes

GiST keeps its tree balanced, at the cost of overlapping subtrees. Many kinds of data, however, can be split into regions that never overlap: a map divided into four quadrants, then each quadrant into four again; a dictionary split by first letter, then by second letter. **SP-GiST** (Space-Partitioned GiST) is a framework for such **space-partitioning trees**: quad-trees, k-d trees, and radix trees (tries). Because partitions do not overlap, a search for a point or a prefix follows exactly one path.

**Two classic shapes**

```text
 Quad-tree for points                        Radix tree (trie) for text
 +-----------+-----------+                   root
 |     .     |  .        |                    +-- "https://"
 |  .   NW   |    NE     |                    |      +-- "shop.example/"
 |           |      .    |                    |      |      +-- "products/" -> entries
 +-----------+-----+-----+                    |      |      +-- "cart"      -> entries
 |           | . . | .   |                    |      +-- "blog.example/"     -> entries
 |    SW     +--+--+-----+                    +-- "http://"  -> entries
 |   .       |  | .|     |
 +-----------+--+--+-----+     each node splits its space; common prefixes are stored once
```

The tree is not balanced: dense areas get deeper subdivisions, sparse ones stay shallow. This suits data with uneven distributions.

**What SP-GiST indexes in core PostgreSQL**

| Operator class | Structure | Supports |
|---|---|---|
| `quad_point_ops` (default for `point`) | Quad-tree | `<@` inside a box, `<<`/`>>` left/right, `~=`, KNN `<->` |
| `kd_point_ops` | k-d tree | Same as above |
| `text_ops` | Radix tree | `=`, `<`, `>`, and prefix search `^@` / `starts_with()` |
| `inet_ops` | Radix tree on network bits | `<<`, `<<=`, `>>`, `>>=`, `&&` |
| `range_ops` | Quad-tree on (lower, upper) | `&&`, `@>`, `<@`, `<<`, `>>`, `-|-` |
| `box_ops`, `poly_ops` | Quad-tree on corners | Box and polygon overlap and containment |

**Prefix search on text.** Long values with shared prefixes, such as URLs or file paths, are stored compactly, because each node keeps only its part of the prefix:

```sql
CREATE INDEX visits_url_spgist ON visits USING spgist (url);

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM visits WHERE url ^@ 'https://shop.example/products/c4ca';   -- "starts with"
--  Aggregate
--    ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on visits
--          Recheck Cond: (url ^@ 'https://shop.example/products/c4ca'::text)
--          ->  Bitmap Index Scan on visits_url_spgist
--                Index Cond: (url ^@ 'https://shop.example/products/c4ca'::text)
```

Unlike a B-tree prefix search with `LIKE 'abc%'`, this works under any collation.

**IP address lookups**

```sql
CREATE TABLE access_log (client_ip inet NOT NULL, requested_at timestamptz NOT NULL);
CREATE INDEX access_log_ip_spgist ON access_log USING spgist (client_ip inet_ops);

SELECT count(*) FROM access_log WHERE client_ip << inet '10.20.0.0/16';   -- IPs inside a subnet
```

**GiST versus SP-GiST**

| | GiST | SP-GiST |
|---|---|---|
| Tree shape | Balanced | Unbalanced, follows the data |
| Sibling regions | May overlap | Never overlap |
| Point and prefix lookups | May search several branches | Follow one path |
| Multicolumn | Yes | No |
| Exclusion constraints | Yes | Yes (with suitable operator classes) |
| Best for | Overlapping objects: shapes, ranges, PostGIS geometries | Points, prefixes, IP networks, skewed distributions |

When both support your data (points, ranges, inet), benchmark both with your queries: SP-GiST is often faster for points and prefixes, GiST for heavily overlapping objects.

**Key takeaways**

- SP-GiST implements non-overlapping, space-partitioning trees: quad-trees, k-d trees, and radix trees.
- Searches for points or prefixes follow a single path, and dense areas are subdivided more deeply.
- Core operator classes cover points, text prefixes (`^@`), `inet` networks, ranges, boxes, and polygons.
- It supports only single-column indexes; choose between it and GiST by data shape and measurement.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create an SP-GiST index on `stores.location` and run the same "nearest five stores" query as in the GiST topic. Compare the index sizes of the two.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Load 1 million random IPv4 addresses into `access_log` and compare a B-tree, a GiST (`inet_ops`), and an SP-GiST index for the query `client_ip << '10.20.0.0/16'`: size, build time, and query time.
> 3. **(Interview)** "What is the difference between a balanced and a space-partitioning tree, and why would a database offer both?" *Hint:* Think about overlapping versus non-overlapping regions, how each behaves with highly skewed data, and which guarantees about search paths each provides.

#### GIN Indexes

Some values are containers: an array of tags, a `jsonb` document with dozens of keys, a `tsvector` with hundreds of words. The typical question is "which rows *contain* this element?" A B-tree on the whole value is useless here, because it sorts entire arrays and documents, not their parts. A **GIN** (Generalized Inverted Index) index flips the relationship: it extracts every element from every value and maps each element to the list of rows that contain it. It is exactly the index at the back of a book: each word, followed by the pages where it appears.

**Structure**

```text
 rows                                            GIN index
 (0,1)  tags = {postgres, sql}                   entry tree (B-tree of keys)
 (0,2)  tags = {sql, tuning}                        |
 (0,3)  tags = {postgres, indexing, tuning}         +-- indexing -> [(0,3)]
                                                    +-- postgres -> [(0,1), (0,3)]
                                                    +-- sql      -> [(0,1), (0,2)]
                                                    +-- tuning   -> [(0,2), (0,3)]
                                                         posting list (compressed);
                                                         a posting tree when very long
```

A query for rows containing `postgres` *and* `tuning` fetches both posting lists and intersects them: only `(0,3)`. Each key is stored once, no matter how many rows contain it, and posting lists are compressed, so GIN indexes on repetitive data are compact.

**What GIN indexes**

| Data | Operator class | Operators |
|---|---|---|
| Arrays | `array_ops` (default) | `@>` contains, `<@` contained by, `&&` overlaps, `=` |
| `jsonb` | `jsonb_ops` (default) | `@>`, `?` key exists, `?|`, `?&`, `@?`, `@@` |
| `jsonb` | `jsonb_path_ops` | `@>`, `@?`, `@@` only, but smaller and faster |
| `tsvector` | `tsvector_ops` | `@@` full-text match ([GIN Indexes for Text Search](#gin-indexes-for-text-search)) |
| `text` with `pg_trgm` | `gin_trgm_ops` | `LIKE '%x%'`, `ILIKE`, `~` regex, `%` similarity ([Trigram Similarity with pg_trgm](#trigram-similarity-with-pg_trgm)) |
| Scalars with `btree_gin` | Various | `=`, `<`, `>`: lets a scalar column join a multicolumn GIN index |

**A jsonb example.** Two percent of `events` belong to a campaign. Without an index, finding them scans every document:

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_payload_gin ON events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"campaign": "black-friday"}';
--  Aggregate
--    ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on events
--          Recheck Cond: (payload @> '{"campaign": "black-friday"}'::jsonb)
--          ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_payload_gin
--                Index Cond: (payload @> '{"campaign": "black-friday"}'::jsonb)
```

The choice between `jsonb_ops` and `jsonb_path_ops`, and indexing single fields instead, is covered in [Indexing JSONB](#indexing-jsonb).

**Characteristics to plan around**

- **Always bitmap scans.** GIN returns an unordered set of `ctid`s. It cannot provide sorted output and does not support index-only scans.
- **Expensive writes.** Inserting one row adds one entry per distinct element, possibly hundreds. With `fastupdate` (on by default), new entries are first appended to a **pending list** and merged in bulk later by vacuum or when the list exceeds `gin_pending_list_limit`, which speeds up inserts but makes some of them slow and makes searches scan the pending list too.
- **Slow to build, fast to search.** Raise `maintenance_work_mem` for large builds; PostgreSQL 18 can also build GIN indexes in parallel.
- **No help for scalar equality.** For `WHERE status = 'paid'`, a B-tree is better.

**Key takeaways**

- GIN is an inverted index: each element (array item, JSON key/value, word, trigram) maps to a compressed list of rows containing it.
- It accelerates containment, overlap, key existence, full-text, and substring (`pg_trgm`) searches.
- It is read only through bitmap scans, without ordering or index-only scans.
- Writes are expensive; the pending list (`fastupdate`) trades steady insert speed for occasional slow merges.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a table of articles with a `tags text[]` column and 100,000 rows, add a GIN index, and compare plans for `tags @> ARRAY['postgres']` and `'postgres' = ANY(tags)`. Which one can use the index?
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build `events_payload_gin` once with `jsonb_ops` and once with `jsonb_path_ops`. Compare sizes, and find a query that only the `jsonb_ops` version can serve.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Inserts into a table with a GIN index are usually fast but occasionally take seconds. What is happening, and what are your options?" *Hint:* Look at the pending list, what triggers its merge, `gin_pending_list_limit`, `fastupdate = off`, and autovacuum settings on that table.

#### BRIN Indexes

The B-tree on `events.created_at` stores one entry for each of the million rows, about 21 MB. Yet `created_at` grows steadily with the physical position of rows: the first pages hold January, the last pages hold December. For such data, a far cheaper summary is enough: "pages 0-127 hold timestamps from January 1 00:00 to January 4 06:00". A **BRIN** (Block Range INdex) stores exactly that: one small summary per range of consecutive pages. To answer a query, PostgreSQL reads the summaries, skips every range that cannot match, and scans only the remaining pages. It is like the labels on archive boxes: "invoices, March 2021". You do not know which page an invoice is on, but you know which boxes to open.

**Structure**

```text
 heap pages:    0 ........ 127 | 128 ...... 255 | 256 ...... 383 | ...
 BRIN entry:    [Jan 1 - Jan 4] [Jan 4 - Jan 8] [Jan 8 - Jan 11]  ...   one min/max per 128 pages

 WHERE created_at BETWEEN 'Jan 5' AND 'Jan 6'
   range 0:   Jan 1 - Jan 4   -> skip
   range 1:   Jan 4 - Jan 8   -> read all 128 pages, recheck every row
   range 2:   Jan 8 - Jan 11  -> skip
```

**Size and usage**

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_created_brin ON events USING brin (created_at);   -- default: 128 pages per range

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('events_created_at_idx')) AS btree,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('events_created_brin'))   AS brin;
--  btree  |  brin
-- --------+-------
--  21 MB  | 24 kB          -- about 900 times smaller

DROP INDEX events_created_at_idx;                    -- so the planner must use the BRIN index
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM events
WHERE created_at >= '2025-06-01' AND created_at < '2025-06-02';
--  Aggregate
--    ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on events
--          Recheck Cond: ((created_at >= ...) AND (created_at < ...))
--          Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 8384    -- rows in the selected ranges that did not match
--          Heap Blocks: lossy=128                 -- whole ranges read, not individual rows
--          ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_created_brin
--                Index Cond: ((created_at >= ...) AND (created_at < ...))
-- (exact numbers vary with your data)
```

BRIN results are always **lossy**: the index identifies page ranges, and every row in those ranges is rechecked. Smaller `pages_per_range` values give more precise but larger indexes:

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_created_brin32 ON events USING brin (created_at) WITH (pages_per_range = 32);
```

**When BRIN works, and when it does not.** BRIN depends entirely on **correlation** between a column's values and the physical row order. Check it before creating the index:

```sql
SELECT attname, correlation FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'events' AND attname IN ('created_at', 'user_id');
--   attname   | correlation
-- ------------+-------------
--  created_at |           1     -- perfect: BRIN works well
--  user_id    |      0.0021     -- random: every range spans almost all user ids; BRIN is useless
```

Good candidates are append-only time series, logs, and sensor readings, along with any monotonically increasing value such as an identity column. Updates and deletes followed by reuse of free space slowly break the correlation.

**Operator classes**

| Class | Summary per range | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `minmax` (default) | Minimum and maximum | Correlated scalar values |
| `minmax_multi` (14+) | Several min/max intervals | Mostly-correlated data with outliers (a few late-arriving rows) |
| `inclusion` | Bounding value (box, range, network) | Geometric types, ranges, `inet` |
| `bloom` (14+) | Bloom filter | Equality on uncorrelated values, such as ids within time-ordered batches |

**Summarizing new pages.** Pages added after the last summarization belong to no summarized range and are always scanned. `VACUUM` (including autovacuum) summarizes them. Creating the index with `WITH (autosummarize = on)` requests summarization as soon as a range fills up, and `brin_summarize_new_values('events_created_brin')` does it manually.

**Key takeaways**

- BRIN stores one small summary (by default min/max) per range of 128 pages, making it hundreds of times smaller than a B-tree.
- It skips ranges that cannot match and rechecks every row in the others, so results are always lossy.
- It works only when values correlate with physical order, as in append-only time-series tables; check `pg_stats.correlation`.
- Tune precision with `pages_per_range`, and keep summaries current with vacuum or `autosummarize`.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a BRIN index on `events.id` and compare its size with `events_pkey`. Run a range query on `id` and check which index the planner picks.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build BRIN indexes on `created_at` with `pages_per_range` of 8, 32, 128, and 512. For a one-hour and a one-week query, record the index size and the `Rows Removed by Index Recheck`. Which setting would you choose, and why?
> 3. **(Interview)** "You have a 5 TB append-only table of sensor readings, queried by time range. The B-tree on the timestamp is 400 GB. What would you do?" *Hint:* Consider BRIN on the timestamp, how late-arriving data affects it, `minmax_multi`, and whether partitioning by time ([6.4](#64-table-partitioning)) would help further.

#### Choosing an Index Type

Each index type answers a different family of questions, so the choice follows from the queries, not from the data type alone. The planner uses an index only if the query's operator belongs to the index's **operator class**. A B-tree on a `jsonb` column cannot help with `@>`, and a GIN index cannot help with `ORDER BY`. Start from the `WHERE` and `ORDER BY` clauses you need to speed up, and pick the index type that supports their operators.

**By query pattern**

| Query pattern | Index type |
|---|---|
| `=`, `<`, `>`, `BETWEEN`, `IN`, `ORDER BY`, `LIKE 'abc%'` on ordinary columns | B-tree |
| Uniqueness (`PRIMARY KEY`, `UNIQUE`) | B-tree (the only option) |
| `=` only, on long values | Hash (or B-tree on `md5(col)`) |
| Overlap, containment, adjacency of ranges; exclusion constraints | GiST (or SP-GiST for ranges) |
| Geometric and geographic searches, nearest neighbors (`<->`) | GiST (PostGIS), SP-GiST for points |
| Prefix search on text (`^@`), IP subnet containment | SP-GiST (or B-tree / GiST) |
| Element containment in arrays, `jsonb` containment and key existence | GIN |
| Full-text search (`@@`) | GIN (GiST for frequently updated, smaller data) |
| Substring and fuzzy text search (`LIKE '%abc%'`, `ILIKE`, similarity) | GIN or GiST with `pg_trgm` |
| Range filters on huge, naturally ordered tables (time series) | BRIN |

**Feature comparison**

| | B-tree | Hash | GiST | SP-GiST | GIN | BRIN |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unique | Yes | No | No | No | No | No |
| Multicolumn | Yes | No | Yes | No | Yes | Yes |
| Sorted output | Yes | No | Distance only (KNN) | Distance only (KNN) | No | No |
| Index-only scans | Yes | No | Some operator classes | Some operator classes | No | No |
| `INCLUDE` columns | Yes | No | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Relative size | Medium | Small to medium | Medium to large | Medium | Small to large | Tiny |
| Write cost | Low | Low | Medium | Medium | High | Very low |

**Decision flow**

```text
 Does the query compare whole scalar values (=, <, >, ORDER BY)?
   yes -> Is the table huge, append-only, and filtered by a column that follows insert order?
            yes -> BRIN (consider B-tree too if queries are very selective)
            no  -> B-tree   (hash only for = on long keys, after measuring)
   no  -> Does it look INSIDE a value (array items, JSON keys, words, substrings)?
            yes -> GIN   (pg_trgm for substrings, tsvector for words)
   no  -> Is it about space or intervals (overlap, containment, distance)?
            yes -> GiST  (SP-GiST for points, prefixes, IP networks)
```

**Asking the catalog.** Operator classes are recorded in the system catalogs. This query lists which index types can serve which operators for a given type:

```sql
SELECT am.amname AS index_type, opf.opfname AS operator_family,
       amop.amopopr::regoperator AS operator
FROM pg_amop AS amop
JOIN pg_opfamily AS opf ON opf.oid = amop.amopfamily
JOIN pg_am AS am        ON am.oid = opf.opfmethod
WHERE amop.amoplefttype = 'jsonb'::regtype
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3;
--  index_type | operator_family |   operator
-- ------------+-----------------+---------------
--  btree      | jsonb_ops       | <(jsonb,jsonb)
--  ...
--  gin        | jsonb_ops       | ?(jsonb,text)
--  gin        | jsonb_ops       | @>(jsonb,jsonb)
--  ...
--  gin        | jsonb_path_ops  | @>(jsonb,jsonb)
--  hash       | jsonb_ops       | =(jsonb,jsonb)
```

**Every index has a price.** Each one slows down inserts and updates of indexed columns, generates WAL, takes disk space and cache memory, and gives vacuum more work. An index nobody uses is pure cost ([Identifying Unused Indexes](#identifying-unused-indexes)). Add indexes for measured needs, not for every column that might be filtered on someday.

**Key takeaways**

- Choose an index type by the operators your queries use; an index helps only if the operator is in its operator class.
- B-tree covers ordinary comparisons and uniqueness; GIN looks inside values; GiST and SP-GiST handle space, ranges, and nearest neighbors; BRIN summarizes huge ordered tables; hash handles equality on long keys.
- Only B-tree supports uniqueness and general sorted output; GIN, BRIN, and hash never support index-only scans.
- Every index costs write speed, space, and maintenance, so add them deliberately.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** For each query, name the index type you would use: `WHERE email = ?`; `WHERE tags && ARRAY['a','b']`; `WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day'` on a 2 TB log table; `WHERE name ILIKE '%phone%'`; `ORDER BY location <-> point(?, ?) LIMIT 5`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Adapt the catalog query to list all operators that a GiST index can support for `tstzrange`, then for `point`, and compare with SP-GiST.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A developer added a GIN index on a `jsonb` column but the query `WHERE payload->>'device' = 'ios'` still scans the table. Why, and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* Check which operators `jsonb_ops` supports, then compare rewriting the query with `@>` against an expression B-tree index on `(payload->>'device')`.

<a id="63-index-design-and-usage"></a>
### 6.3 Index Design and Usage

This subchapter turns index mechanics into design decisions: how many columns to index and in which order, how to index only part of a table or a computed value, how to let queries skip the table entirely, and how to build, maintain, and retire indexes on a live system. The examples use the `events` table from [6.1](#61-physical-storage-layout). To start from a clean state, drop the indexes created in [6.2](#62-index-structures):

```sql
DROP INDEX IF EXISTS events_user_id_idx, events_created_at_idx, events_payload_gin,
                     events_created_brin, events_created_brin32;
-- events_pkey (on id) remains
```

#### Single vs. Multicolumn Indexes

Real queries rarely filter on a single column: "this user's events in the last week", "paid orders in Germany". You can serve such queries with one index per column, or with one index that contains several columns. The two approaches behave differently, and choosing well avoids both slow queries and a pile of indexes that slow down every write.

**Option 1: several single-column indexes, combined at run time.** The planner can scan several indexes, turn each result into a bitmap of matching pages, and combine the bitmaps with AND or OR before touching the table:

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_user_id_idx ON events (user_id);
CREATE INDEX events_created_at_idx ON events (created_at);

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 4242 OR id = 17;
--  Bitmap Heap Scan on events
--    Recheck Cond: ((user_id = 4242) OR (id = 17))
--    ->  BitmapOr                                          -- union of both bitmaps
--          ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_user_id_idx
--                Index Cond: (user_id = 4242)
--          ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_pkey
--                Index Cond: (id = 17)

-- With AND, the same mechanism produces a BitmapAnd when each condition alone matches
-- many rows but together they match few (the planner decides from statistics):
--  Bitmap Heap Scan on events
--    ->  BitmapAnd
--          ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_user_id_idx
--          ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_created_at_idx
```

**Option 2: one multicolumn (composite) index.** An index on `(user_id, created_at)` stores entries sorted by `user_id`, and by `created_at` within each user. A query with both conditions descends once and reads only the matching entries:

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_user_created_idx ON events (user_id, created_at);

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 4242 AND created_at >= '2025-06-01';
--  Index Scan using events_user_created_idx on events
--    Index Cond: ((user_id = 4242) AND (created_at >= '2025-06-01 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone))
```

**Comparison**

| | Several single-column indexes | One multicolumn index |
|---|---|---|
| Queries served | Any combination of the indexed columns | Queries matching the index's leading columns ([next topic](#column-order-in-composite-indexes)) |
| Efficiency for the combined condition | Scans each index fully for its condition, then combines bitmaps | One descent, reads only matching entries |
| Sorted output (`ORDER BY ... LIMIT`) | Bitmap scans return no order | Can return rows in index order |
| Index-only scans | Not when combining | Yes, if it holds all needed columns |
| Write cost and space | One index per column | One index |

**Guidelines**

- Start from the queries, not the columns. A frequent, important query with a fixed combination of conditions deserves a composite index shaped for it.
- Single-column indexes on separately filtered columns are a flexible fallback for ad hoc combinations.
- A composite index on `(a, b)` also serves queries on `a` alone, so a separate index on `a` is usually redundant.
- Indexes can have up to 32 columns, but more than three or four key columns is rarely useful.

**Key takeaways**

- The planner can combine single-column indexes with `BitmapAnd`/`BitmapOr`, at the cost of scanning each one for its condition.
- A composite index serves a specific combination of conditions with one descent, and can provide ordering and index-only scans.
- A composite index on `(a, b)` makes a separate index on `(a)` redundant.
- Design composite indexes for your most important queries; keep the total number of indexes small.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** With only `events_user_id_idx` and `events_created_at_idx` present, run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` for `user_id = 4242 AND created_at >= '2025-06-01'`. Then create `events_user_created_idx` and compare the plans and timings.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Find a pair of conditions on `events` for which the planner chooses a `BitmapAnd`. Explain from the row estimates why it prefers combining two indexes over using only one.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A table has eight single-column indexes, one for each filterable column in the UI. Is that a good design?" *Hint:* Consider write cost, which combinations users actually run, how bitmap combination performs for each, and what you would measure before changing it.

#### Column Order in Composite Indexes

A phone book is sorted by last name, then first name. Finding "Smith, Anna" is instant; finding every "Smith" is instant; but finding every "Anna" means reading the whole book, because the Annas are scattered among all the last names. A composite B-tree index behaves exactly the same way. It is one sorted list ordered by the first column, then by the second within equal first values, and so on. Which queries it can serve efficiently depends on the column order.

**The sorted list for `(user_id, created_at)`**

```text
  (4241, 2025-02-11)
  (4241, 2025-09-30)
  (4242, 2025-01-07)   <-+
  (4242, 2025-03-19)     |  user_id = 4242: one contiguous block
  (4242, 2025-06-02)  <--|--+
  (4242, 2025-08-14)     |  |  user_id = 4242 AND created_at >= '2025-06-01':
  (4242, 2025-11-23)   <-+--+  a contiguous sub-block
  (4243, 2025-01-30)
  (4243, 2025-07-05)
  ...                         created_at >= '2025-06-01' alone: scattered across ALL users
```

**The leftmost-prefix rule**

| Condition | Can use `(user_id, created_at)` efficiently? |
|---|---|
| `user_id = 4242` | Yes: a prefix of the index |
| `user_id = 4242 AND created_at >= '2025-06-01'` | Yes: equality on the first column, range on the second |
| `user_id IN (1, 2, 3) AND created_at >= ...` | Yes: one descent per value |
| `user_id BETWEEN 4000 AND 4100 AND created_at >= ...` | Partly: the range on `user_id` is used to find entries, `created_at` is checked on each entry inside it |
| `created_at >= '2025-06-01'` alone | Not efficiently (but see skip scan below) |

**Equality first, range last.** Once a range condition is applied to a column, the entries matching the following columns are no longer contiguous. For a query `WHERE kind = 'refund' AND created_at >= '2025-11-01'`, compare:

```text
 (kind, created_at): equality first           (created_at, kind): range first
   ('purchase', ...)                            ('2025-11-01 00:00', 'view')
   ('refund', 2025-10-30)                       ('2025-11-01 00:00', 'refund')   <- match
   ('refund', 2025-11-02)  <- start here        ('2025-11-01 00:01', 'click')
   ('refund', 2025-11-05)     read only         ('2025-11-01 00:01', 'view')
   ('refund', 2025-12-28)  <- matches           ... every entry since Nov 1 must be read,
   ('view', ...)                                    and 99.5 % of them are discarded
```

The rule of thumb is: **columns compared with `=` first, then at most one column compared with a range**. The often-quoted advice "put the most selective column first" is secondary: for a query with equality on both columns, both orders read exactly the same entries. Order among equality columns matters for *other* queries that use only a prefix of the index.

**Serving ORDER BY.** Because entries for one `user_id` are already sorted by `created_at`, the index can return a user's latest events without a sort step, and stop after the `LIMIT`:

```sql
DROP INDEX events_user_id_idx;              -- redundant: (user_id, created_at) covers it

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 4242 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;
--  Limit
--    ->  Index Scan Backward using events_user_created_idx on events
--          Index Cond: (user_id = 4242)            -- no Sort node: rows arrive in order
```

This is the pattern behind fast feeds, timelines, and keyset pagination ([Keyset Pagination](#keyset-pagination)). With mixed directions, such as `ORDER BY user_id, created_at DESC` across many users, the index must be declared with matching directions, `(user_id, created_at DESC)`, or with both directions reversed.

**Skip scan (PostgreSQL 18+).** Since version 18, a B-tree can be used even when the leading column has no condition, by "skipping" through each distinct value of that column and searching inside each one. It pays off only when the leading column has few distinct values:

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_kind_created_idx ON events (kind, created_at);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2025-12-30';     -- no condition on kind
--  Aggregate
--    ->  Index Only Scan using events_kind_created_idx on events
--          Index Cond: (created_at >= '2025-12-30 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone)
--          Index Searches: 4                   -- one descent per distinct kind value
--          ...
```

With `user_id` (100,000 distinct values) leading, a skip scan would need 100,000 descents, so the planner will not choose it. Do not rely on skip scan as a design principle; it is a safety net that makes some extra queries cheap.

**Key takeaways**

- A composite B-tree is sorted by the first column, then the second, and so on; conditions on a leading prefix are efficient.
- Put columns compared with `=` first and at most one range column last.
- Matching column order and direction lets an index satisfy `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` without sorting.
- PostgreSQL 18's skip scan helps queries that omit a leading column with few distinct values, but does not replace good ordering.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** With an index on `(country, kind)`, predict which of these queries can use it efficiently, then check with `EXPLAIN`: `country = 'JP'`; `kind = 'refund'`; `country = 'JP' AND kind = 'refund'`; `kind = 'refund' AND country IN ('JP', 'DE')`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Design one index that serves both "the last 20 purchases of a user" and "the number of purchases of a user in a date range", and verify both plans.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Should the most selective column always come first in a composite index?" *Hint:* Separate the cost for a query with equality on all columns from the reuse of the index by other queries, and consider where range conditions must go.

#### Partial Indexes

Indexes usually cover every row, but queries often care about a small, well-defined subset: the 0.5 % of events that are refunds, orders still `pending`, rows not soft-deleted. Indexing the other 99 % wastes space, cache memory, and write time on entries no query will ever read. A **partial index** has a `WHERE` clause and contains entries only for rows that satisfy it.

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_refunds_idx ON events (created_at) WHERE kind = 'refund';

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('events_refunds_idx'));
-- about 150 kB       (5,000 refund rows, versus ~21 MB for created_at on all rows)
```

**When the planner can use it.** The planner uses a partial index only if it can *prove* that the query's `WHERE` clause implies the index's predicate. The proof is logical, not statistical, and works on simple forms:

```sql
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM events WHERE kind = 'refund' AND created_at >= '2025-12-01';
--  Index Scan using events_refunds_idx on events                 -- query implies kind = 'refund'
--    Index Cond: (created_at >= '2025-12-01 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone)

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM events WHERE kind IN ('refund', 'purchase') AND created_at >= '2025-12-01';
-- the partial index cannot be used: the query also needs purchases
```

**Prepared statements.** With a parameter, `WHERE kind = $1` proves nothing until the value is known. A custom plan (made with the actual value) can use the partial index; a generic plan, which the plan cache may switch to after five executions, cannot. If the predicate is fixed in your application, write it as a literal in the query rather than as a parameter.

**Common uses**

| Need | Partial index |
|---|---|
| Find rare rows quickly | `ON orders (placed_at) WHERE status = 'pending'` |
| Skip mostly-`NULL` columns | `ON orders (shipped_at) WHERE shipped_at IS NOT NULL` |
| Soft deletes: index only live rows | `ON documents (owner_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` |
| Unique among a subset | `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` |
| Job queues: only unprocessed work | `ON jobs (priority, created_at) WHERE finished_at IS NULL` |

The unique variant enforces a rule that no constraint can express: an email address may appear once among active users, while any number of deleted users may share it.

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id         bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email      text NOT NULL,
  deleted_at timestamptz
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_active_email_uq ON users (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

INSERT INTO users (email, deleted_at) VALUES ('ana@example.com', now());   -- deleted account
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('Ana@example.com');                      -- OK: the first one is deleted
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('ana@EXAMPLE.com');
-- ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "users_active_email_uq"
```

**Avoid over-partitioning.** Do not create one partial index per value (`WHERE kind = 'view'`, `WHERE kind = 'click'`, ...) as a substitute for an index on `(kind, ...)`. Partial indexes shine when the predicate selects a small, stable subset that queries name explicitly.

**Key takeaways**

- A partial index stores entries only for rows matching its `WHERE` clause, making it small and cheap to maintain.
- The planner uses it only when it can prove the query's conditions imply the index predicate.
- Parameters in the predicate column can defeat partial indexes in generic plans.
- Partial unique indexes enforce uniqueness within a subset, such as active rows.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a partial index on `orders (placed_at) WHERE status = 'pending'` and write two queries: one that can use it and one that cannot.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Create `events_refunds_idx`, then `PREPARE` a query with `WHERE kind = $1 AND created_at >= $2`. Execute it with `SET plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan` and with `force_custom_plan`, and compare the plans.
> 3. **(Interview)** "How would you build a job queue table in PostgreSQL where workers repeatedly fetch the oldest unprocessed job, and the table holds 100 million finished jobs?" *Hint:* Consider a partial index on unprocessed rows, `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and what happens to the index as jobs are completed.

#### Expression Indexes

An index on `email` stores the values as written. A query like `WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'` asks about a *computed* value, which is not in the index, so the planner must compute `lower(email)` for every row ([4.2](#42-expressions-and-functions)). An **expression index** (or functional index) stores the result of an expression instead of a raw column, so queries that use the same expression can search it directly.

```sql
CREATE INDEX customers_email_lower_idx ON customers (lower(email));

-- On a large customers table:
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com';
--  Index Scan using customers_email_lower_idx on customers
--    Index Cond: (lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'::text)
```

**Syntax.** A function call can be written directly; any other expression needs an extra pair of parentheses:

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_device_idx ON events ((payload->>'device'));                -- operator: double parentheses
CREATE INDEX events_day_idx ON events (((created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date)); -- cast: double parentheses
```

**The query must use the same expression.** The planner matches expressions structurally. `lower(email)` in the index does not help `WHERE upper(email) = ...`, and `(payload->>'device')` does not help `payload @> '{"device": "ios"}'`.

```sql
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date = '2025-06-01';
--  Aggregate
--    ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on events
--          Recheck Cond: (((created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'::text))::date = '2025-06-01'::date)
--          ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_day_idx
```

**Only IMMUTABLE functions.** An index entry is computed once, when the row is written. If the function could return a different result later for the same input, the index would silently become wrong. PostgreSQL therefore accepts only functions marked `IMMUTABLE` ([9.1](#91-functions-and-procedures)):

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON events (date_trunc('day', created_at));
-- ERROR:  functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE
-- date_trunc on timestamptz depends on the session's TimeZone setting, so it is only STABLE.
-- Fix: make the time zone explicit, as in events_day_idx above.
```

Never mark your own function `IMMUTABLE` just to get past this error if it reads tables or settings. The index will return wrong results when the underlying data changes.

**Statistics come for free.** After `ANALYZE`, PostgreSQL collects statistics on each indexed expression, so the planner can estimate how many rows `lower(email) = ...` matches, which improves plans even beyond the index itself.

**Expression index or generated column?**

| | Expression index | Stored generated column + plain index |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | Only in the index | In the table and the index |
| Query must write | The exact expression | The column name |
| Visible to applications | No | Yes, like any column |
| Usable for index-only scans | Limited | Yes |

**Key takeaways**

- An expression index stores computed values, such as `lower(email)` or `payload->>'device'`, so filters on that expression can use an index.
- Queries must use exactly the indexed expression to benefit.
- Only `IMMUTABLE` functions are allowed; time-zone-dependent operations need an explicit time zone.
- The expression is computed on every insert and update, and `ANALYZE` gathers statistics on it.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create an expression index for case-insensitive lookup of `products.sku` and verify it is used with `SET enable_seqscan = off` (the table is small).
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Index `events` so that "count of events per day for one country" uses an index. Compare an expression index on the UTC date with a stored generated column.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why does PostgreSQL reject `CREATE INDEX ON orders (date_trunc('month', placed_at))` when `placed_at` is `timestamptz`, but accept it for `timestamp`?" *Hint:* Think about what `date_trunc` needs to know about time zones in each case and what `IMMUTABLE` promises.

#### Covering Indexes with INCLUDE

An ordinary index scan finds matching entries in the index, then visits the heap for each one to get the remaining columns. When a query needs only one or two extra columns, those heap visits can dominate the cost. If the index itself held those columns, the query could be answered from the index alone, with an **index-only scan** ([Index-Only Scans](#index-only-scans)). Since PostgreSQL 11, the `INCLUDE` clause adds such "passenger" columns to an index without making them part of the key.

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_user_created_incl ON events (user_id, created_at) INCLUDE (kind, amount);

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT created_at, kind, amount FROM events WHERE user_id = 4242;
--  Index Only Scan using events_user_created_incl on events      -- no heap access needed
--    Index Cond: (user_id = 4242)
```

**Key columns versus INCLUDE columns.** Why not simply add `kind` and `amount` as key columns?

| | Key column | `INCLUDE` column |
|---|---|---|
| Stored in | Leaf and internal pages | Leaf pages only (smaller upper levels) |
| Defines sort order | Yes | No |
| Usable in `Index Cond` (to find entries) | Yes | No, only returned (or filtered after finding) |
| Part of uniqueness check | Yes | No |
| Requires a B-tree operator class | Yes | No: any type can be included |

The uniqueness difference is often the deciding one. A unique index on `sku` that also carries `price` must keep `sku` alone as the key:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX products_sku_incl ON products (sku) INCLUDE (price);
-- unique on sku only; SELECT price FROM products WHERE sku = 'BK-001' can be an index-only scan
-- an index UNIQUE (sku, price) would allow two rows with the same sku and different prices
```

**Costs**

- **Larger index.** Every included column is copied into every leaf entry. Including wide columns (`text` descriptions, `jsonb`) can make the index nearly as big as the table.
- **No HOT updates on those columns.** An `UPDATE` that changes an included column must update the index, exactly as for a key column ([Heap File Organization](#heap-file-organization)).
- **Only B-tree, GiST, and SP-GiST** support `INCLUDE`.
- **Still needs the visibility map.** Index-only scans skip the heap only for all-visible pages, so a covering index on a frequently changing table may still do many heap fetches.

**Key takeaways**

- `INCLUDE` adds non-key columns to an index's leaf entries so queries can be answered by index-only scans.
- Included columns do not affect ordering or uniqueness and do not need a B-tree operator class.
- Use them for a few small columns returned by important, frequent queries.
- Each included column enlarges the index and prevents HOT updates when it changes.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create `products_sku_incl` and use `EXPLAIN` to confirm an index-only scan for `SELECT price FROM products WHERE sku = 'BK-001'` (use `SET enable_seqscan = off` on the small table).
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Compare the size of `(user_id, created_at) INCLUDE (kind, amount)` with `(user_id, created_at, kind, amount)` and with `(user_id, created_at)`. Then list queries the four-column key index can serve that the `INCLUDE` version cannot.
> 3. **(Interview)** "When would you prefer adding a column to an index's `INCLUDE` list over adding it as a key column?" *Hint:* Consider uniqueness semantics, whether the column is ever filtered or sorted on, its data type, and the size of internal pages.

#### Unique Indexes and Constraints

A rule such as "no two products share a SKU" must hold even when two transactions insert the same SKU at the same instant. Checking with a `SELECT` first is not enough: both transactions may see no duplicate and both insert. PostgreSQL enforces uniqueness inside the index itself: inserting into a **unique B-tree index** checks for an existing live entry with the same key and, if another transaction is inserting the same key concurrently, waits for it to commit or roll back. This is why every `PRIMARY KEY` and `UNIQUE` constraint ([2.2](#22-keys-and-integrity)) is backed by a unique index.

**Constraint versus index.** There are two ways to get uniqueness, with different capabilities:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD CONSTRAINT products_name_key UNIQUE (name);   -- a constraint (creates its own index)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX products_name_lower_uq ON products (lower(name));  -- only an index
```

| | `UNIQUE` / `PRIMARY KEY` constraint | `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` |
|---|---|---|
| Expressions (`lower(email)`) | No | Yes |
| Partial (`WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`) | No | Yes |
| Can be `DEFERRABLE` | Yes | No |
| Target of a foreign key | Yes | Yes, if plain columns and not partial |
| Listed in `information_schema` / used by ORMs | Yes | No |
| `ON CONFLICT` target | Yes | Yes |

Prefer a constraint when plain columns are enough; it documents intent and supports deferral. Use a unique index for expressions and subsets.

**NULLs are distinct by default.** Two rows with `NULL` in a unique column do not conflict, because `NULL` is not equal to `NULL`. Since PostgreSQL 15, `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` treats them as equal:

```sql
CREATE TABLE coupons (
  code        text,
  customer_id bigint,
  UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (code, customer_id)   -- at most one generic coupon (customer_id NULL) per code
);
```

**Immediate checks and deferrable constraints.** A non-deferrable unique constraint is checked for each row *as it is modified*, not at the end of the statement. Statements that pass through a temporary duplicate fail even though the final result is valid:

```sql
CREATE TABLE playlist_items (
  playlist_id int,
  position    int,
  song        text,
  UNIQUE (playlist_id, position)
);
INSERT INTO playlist_items VALUES (1, 1, 'Intro'), (1, 2, 'Verse'), (1, 3, 'Outro');

UPDATE playlist_items SET position = position + 1 WHERE playlist_id = 1;
-- ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "playlist_items_playlist_id_position_key"
-- DETAIL:  Key (playlist_id, "position")=(1, 2) already exists.     <- row 1 moved onto row 2's position

ALTER TABLE playlist_items
  DROP CONSTRAINT playlist_items_playlist_id_position_key,
  ADD CONSTRAINT playlist_items_pos_key UNIQUE (playlist_id, position) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE;

UPDATE playlist_items SET position = position + 1 WHERE playlist_id = 1;   -- OK: checked at statement end
```

`DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE` checks at the end of each statement; `SET CONSTRAINTS ... DEFERRED` postpones the check to `COMMIT`. Deferrable checks are somewhat slower, and a deferrable constraint cannot be used as an `ON CONFLICT` arbiter.

**Adding uniqueness to a large live table.** `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE` builds the index while blocking writes. Build the index concurrently first ([Concurrent Index Creation](#concurrent-index-creation)), then attach it as a constraint, which is nearly instant:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_uq ON users (email);
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT users_email_key UNIQUE USING INDEX users_email_uq;
-- NOTICE: the index is renamed to "users_email_key"
```

**Key takeaways**

- Uniqueness is enforced by unique B-tree indexes, which handle concurrent inserts correctly; constraints create one automatically.
- Use constraints for plain columns (deferrable, FK targets, visible to tools); use unique indexes for expressions and partial uniqueness.
- `NULL`s never conflict unless the constraint uses `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PostgreSQL 15+).
- Non-deferrable unique checks happen row by row; use `DEFERRABLE` for updates that pass through temporary duplicates.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Try inserting two customers with `NULL` emails into the shop schema. Then explain how you would allow at most one customer without an email.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Reproduce the `playlist_items` error, then find a way to shift positions *without* making the constraint deferrable (for example, in two `UPDATE` statements).
> 3. **(Interview)** "Two application servers check whether a username exists and insert it if not. Occasionally duplicates appear. How do you fix it?" *Hint:* Discuss why check-then-insert races, what a unique index guarantees under concurrency, and how `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` makes the operation a single atomic step.

#### Index-Only Scans

An index entry contains the key and a `ctid`, but not the information needed to decide whether its row is visible to the current transaction: `xmin` and `xmax` live only in the heap ([Tuple Headers and Visibility Info](#tuple-headers-and-visibility-info)). A normal index scan therefore always visits the heap. An **index-only scan** avoids that visit when two conditions hold: every column the query needs is in the index, and the visibility map says the heap page is **all-visible**, so every row on it is visible to everyone ([Free Space Map and Visibility Map](#free-space-map-and-visibility-map)).

```text
 for each matching index entry:
    is the entry's heap page marked all-visible in the VM?
       yes -> return the values straight from the index             (no heap I/O)
       no  -> fetch the heap tuple to check visibility ("heap fetch")
```

**Seeing it in a plan.** `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` reports how many entries still needed the heap:

```sql
-- events_user_created_incl from the previous topic: (user_id, created_at) INCLUDE (kind, amount)
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
SELECT created_at, kind FROM events WHERE user_id = 4242;
--  Index Only Scan using events_user_created_incl on events (actual rows=9 loops=1)
--    Index Cond: (user_id = 4242)
--    Heap Fetches: 0                        -- the table was vacuumed: every page all-visible

UPDATE events SET amount = amount WHERE user_id = 4242;   -- touches ~9 heap pages, clearing their VM bits

-- run the same EXPLAIN again
--    Heap Fetches: 18                       -- old and new versions now need visibility checks

VACUUM events;
-- run it again
--    Heap Fetches: 0
```

**When index-only scans pay off**

- Frequent queries that read a few columns, matched by a covering index.
- `count(*)` with a condition on an indexed column, which needs no columns at all.
- Tables that are mostly read, or regularly vacuumed. On a table where most pages change between vacuums, an index-only scan degrades to an ordinary index scan.

**Keeping the visibility map current.** Autovacuum triggers by default after a fraction of rows has been *updated or deleted*. Since PostgreSQL 13, it also runs on tables that receive many *inserts* (`autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold` and `autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor`), so append-only tables also get their pages marked all-visible. For tables where index-only scans matter, lowering the scale factors makes vacuum run more often ([8.5](#85-vacuum-and-maintenance)):

```sql
ALTER TABLE events SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02,
                        autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor = 0.02);
```

**Limitations**

- Not available for GIN, BRIN, or hash indexes, which do not store the original values.
- GiST and SP-GiST support it only for some operator classes.
- For an expression index, the planner may still want the underlying column; adding that column with `INCLUDE` works around it.
- The planner estimates heap fetches from `pg_class.relallvisible`. Stale statistics after a big data change can lead it to avoid an index-only scan that would have been fine.

**Key takeaways**

- An index-only scan returns data from the index alone when all needed columns are in it and the heap page is all-visible.
- `Heap Fetches` in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` counts entries that still required a heap visit.
- Vacuum keeps the visibility map current; tune autovacuum on tables that rely on index-only scans.
- Only B-tree reliably supports them; GiST and SP-GiST partly; GIN, BRIN, and hash never.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE user_id BETWEEN 1 AND 1000` and check whether it is an index-only scan and how many heap fetches it makes.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Update 10 % of `events` at random, then measure the query above before and after `VACUUM`, recording heap fetches and execution time.
> 3. **(Interview)** "An index-only scan in production shows `Heap Fetches` equal to the number of rows returned. What does this tell you and what would you do?" *Hint:* Think about the visibility map, how often the table is modified, when autovacuum last ran (`pg_stat_user_tables.last_autovacuum`), and long-running transactions that prevent vacuum from marking pages all-visible.

#### Concurrent Index Creation

A plain `CREATE INDEX` reads the whole table and writes a sorted index. To make sure no rows are missed while it reads, it takes a `SHARE` lock on the table for the entire build. Reads continue, but every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` waits. On a 500 GB table, that can be an outage of an hour or more. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` builds the index *while writes continue*, in exchange for doing more work and taking longer.

**How it works.** It takes a weaker `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` lock, which does not block writes, and builds the index in phases:

```text
 1. Create the index in the catalog, marked invalid      -> new transactions start maintaining it
 2. Wait for transactions that might not know about the index yet ("waiting for writers")
 3. Scan the table and build the index                    (writes continue during this phase)
 4. Wait again, then scan the table a second time and add rows written during step 3
 5. Wait for transactions whose snapshots predate the build, then mark the index valid
```

```sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_country_idx ON events (country);

-- In another session, follow its progress:
SELECT phase, blocks_done, blocks_total, tuples_done, tuples_total
FROM pg_stat_progress_create_index;
--        phase        | blocks_done | blocks_total | tuples_done | tuples_total
-- --------------------+-------------+--------------+-------------+--------------
--  building index: scanning table |     5210 |    11312 |           0 |            0
```

**Restrictions and failure modes**

- **Not inside a transaction block.** `BEGIN; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ...` fails with `ERROR: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block`. Migration tools that wrap each migration in a transaction need an option to disable that for these steps.
- **It waits for old transactions.** A long-running transaction or an idle-in-transaction session elsewhere stalls phases 2, 4, and 5 until it ends.
- **Failure leaves an invalid index.** If the build fails (a deadlock, a uniqueness violation, a cancellation), the index remains, marked `INVALID`. It is not used for queries but is still maintained on every write. Drop it and retry, or rebuild it:

```sql
SELECT indexrelid::regclass AS index_name
FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;          -- find invalid indexes
--     index_name
-- -------------------
--  events_country_idx

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_country_idx;   -- then run CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY again
-- or: REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_country_idx;
```

**The CONCURRENTLY family**

| Command | Purpose | Since |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` | Build without blocking writes | 8.2 |
| `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` | Drop without blocking queries on the table | 9.2 |
| `REINDEX ... CONCURRENTLY` | Rebuild without blocking writes | 12 |
| `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX` | Turn a concurrently built unique index into a constraint | 9.1 |

**Speeding up builds.** Index builds sort data in memory up to `maintenance_work_mem`, and can use parallel workers (`max_parallel_maintenance_workers`) for B-tree, BRIN (17+), and GIN (18+):

```sql
SET maintenance_work_mem = '2GB';                -- this session only
SET max_parallel_maintenance_workers = 4;
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_amount_idx ON events (amount);
```

**Key takeaways**

- Plain `CREATE INDEX` blocks writes for the whole build; `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` does not, at the cost of two table scans and waiting for older transactions.
- It cannot run inside a transaction block, and long-running transactions stall it.
- A failed concurrent build leaves an `INVALID` index that still slows writes; find it in `pg_index` and drop or rebuild it.
- Use `CONCURRENTLY` for every index change on live production tables.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** In one session, start `CREATE INDEX` (without `CONCURRENTLY`) on a 10-million-row table; in another, try an `INSERT`. Repeat with `CONCURRENTLY` and compare.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Open a transaction in one session and leave it idle. In another, start `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and use `pg_stat_progress_create_index` and `pg_stat_activity` to find what it is waiting for.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your migration added a unique index concurrently, it failed halfway because of a duplicate, and now inserts are slower. Explain what happened and how to recover." *Hint:* Consider what an invalid index still costs, how to find it, how to find and fix the duplicates, and how to retry safely.

#### Index Bloat and Maintenance

Indexes do not shrink by themselves. When rows are deleted or updated, their old index entries become dead. Vacuum removes them, but the space they occupied stays inside the index's pages, and B-tree pages are reclaimed only when they become *completely* empty. After heavy updates or deletes spread across the key space, an index can end up with mostly-empty pages: it is **bloated**. A bloated index is larger than needed, takes more cache memory, and makes range scans read more pages.

**A demonstration**

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;

CREATE TABLE bloat_demo (id int PRIMARY KEY, v text);
INSERT INTO bloat_demo SELECT g, md5(g::text) FROM generate_series(1, 1000000) AS g;

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('bloat_demo_pkey'));       -- 21 MB

DELETE FROM bloat_demo WHERE id % 10 <> 0;   -- delete 90 % of rows, spread over every leaf page
VACUUM bloat_demo;

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('bloat_demo_pkey'));       -- still 21 MB
SELECT leaf_pages, avg_leaf_density, leaf_fragmentation
FROM pgstatindex('bloat_demo_pkey');
--  leaf_pages | avg_leaf_density | leaf_fragmentation
-- ------------+------------------+--------------------
--        2733 |              9.1 |                  0     -- pages are ~9 % full

REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY bloat_demo_pkey;
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('bloat_demo_pkey'));       -- ~2.2 MB
```

**Built-in defenses.** Several mechanisms limit bloat without any action on your part:

| Mechanism | What it does |
|---|---|
| HOT updates | Updates that change no indexed column add no index entries at all ([Heap File Organization](#heap-file-organization)) |
| Killed index tuples | An index scan that finds an entry pointing to a dead row marks it, so later scans skip it and inserts can reuse its space |
| Deduplication (13+) | Repeated keys share one entry with a list of `ctid`s |
| Bottom-up deletion (14+) | Before splitting a full page, removes entries for versions created by non-HOT updates |
| Vacuum | Removes dead entries and recycles empty pages |

**Measuring bloat.** `pgstatindex` reads the whole index and reports exact density, so run it carefully on large indexes. A quicker rule: compare the index size with its expected size after a rebuild, or with the size of an identical index built on a recent copy. An `avg_leaf_density` well below the fillfactor (90 for B-trees) on a large, frequently scanned index is a sign of bloat.

**Fixing it**

```sql
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_user_created_incl;   -- one index, writes continue (12+)
REINDEX TABLE CONCURRENTLY events;                     -- all indexes of a table
```

`REINDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY` blocks writes to the table and blocks queries that would use the index. For bloated *tables*, `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table but holds an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for the whole operation; the `pg_repack` extension does the same online ([13.2](#132-notable-extensions)).

**Index fillfactor.** B-tree leaves are filled to 90 % on creation, leaving room for inserts in the middle of the key range. For keys that only ever increase (identity columns, timestamps), `fillfactor = 100` saves space; for random keys with heavy updates, a lower fillfactor reduces page splits:

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_created_ff ON events (created_at) WITH (fillfactor = 100);
```

**Key takeaways**

- Index bloat comes from deletes and non-HOT updates leaving partially empty pages that are not merged.
- HOT updates, deduplication, bottom-up deletion, and vacuum limit it automatically.
- Measure with `pgstatindex` or by comparing with a freshly built index; fix with `REINDEX ... CONCURRENTLY`.
- Use fillfactor deliberately: 100 for ever-increasing keys, lower for random keys with many updates.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run the `bloat_demo` example and record the index size and `avg_leaf_density` at each step.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Instead of deleting every tenth row, delete the *first* 90 % of ids and vacuum. Compare the index size and `pgstatindex` output with the scattered delete, and explain the difference.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Index sizes on a busy table keep growing even though the row count is stable. How would you investigate?" *Hint:* Check the HOT update ratio, which columns are updated and indexed, autovacuum activity, long-running transactions that keep dead rows alive, and `pgstatindex` results over time.

#### Identifying Unused Indexes

Indexes accumulate. A developer adds one to fix a slow query, the query is rewritten a year later, and the index stays forever. Every unused index still has to be updated on each insert and on each update of its columns, generates WAL, takes space and cache memory, slows vacuum, and can prevent HOT updates. Finding and removing indexes that no query uses is one of the cheapest performance wins in a mature database.

**Usage statistics.** PostgreSQL counts how often each index is scanned in `pg_stat_user_indexes`:

```sql
SELECT s.relname AS table_name,
       s.indexrelname AS index_name,
       s.idx_scan,                                       -- scans since statistics were last reset
       s.last_idx_scan,                                  -- PostgreSQL 16+
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS index_size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes AS s
JOIN pg_index AS i ON i.indexrelid = s.indexrelid
WHERE s.idx_scan = 0
  AND NOT i.indisunique                                  -- unique indexes enforce rules even if never scanned
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint AS c       -- nor drop indexes backing exclusion constraints
                  WHERE c.conindid = s.indexrelid)
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;
--  table_name |     index_name      | idx_scan | last_idx_scan | index_size
-- ------------+---------------------+----------+---------------+------------
--  events     | events_country_idx  |        0 |               | 7008 kB
--  events     | events_amount_idx   |        0 |               | 6760 kB
```

**Before dropping, check these traps**

| Trap | Why it misleads | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Statistics were reset recently | `idx_scan = 0` may only cover a few hours | Check `stats_reset` in `pg_stat_database`; observe over weeks |
| Replicas | Statistics are per server; an index unused on the primary may serve read queries on a replica | Run the query on every server |
| Rare but critical queries | Month-end reports, yearly jobs, incident-time queries | Look at a full business cycle; ask the owners |
| Constraint enforcement | Unique, primary key, and exclusion indexes do their main job without "scans" | Never drop them based on `idx_scan` |
| Foreign keys | An index on a referencing column speeds up deletes in the referenced table, which may show few scans | Keep FK indexes on tables whose parents are deleted from |

**Duplicate and redundant indexes.** Two indexes with identical definitions are pure waste, and an index on `(a)` is usually redundant next to one on `(a, b)`:

```sql
-- Exact duplicates: same table, columns, operator classes, expressions, and predicate
SELECT indrelid::regclass AS table_name,
       array_agg(indexrelid::regclass) AS duplicate_indexes
FROM pg_index
```
