PostgreSQL's built-in logging (`log_statement`) records statement text, but is coarse, hard to parse, and misses what a statement touched indirectly. Audit triggers ([Audit Logging with Triggers](#audit-logging-with-triggers)) record data changes but not reads or DDL. The **pgaudit** extension produces detailed, structured audit records of sessions and object access through the standard server log.

**Analogy.** Normal logging is a security camera pointed at the front door; pgaudit is a sign-out sheet attached to every sensitive cabinet, filled in automatically with who opened it, which folder they took, and when.

**Installation**

```ini
# postgresql.conf (restart required)
shared_preload_libraries = 'pgaudit'
pgaudit.log = 'ddl, role, write'          # session audit classes, see below
pgaudit.log_relation = on                 # one entry per table touched, not just per statement
pgaudit.log_parameter = off               # parameters may contain sensitive data; enable consciously
log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %q%u@%d %r %a '  # time, pid, user@db, client address, application
log_connections = on
log_disconnections = on
```

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION pgaudit;                  -- in each database where you want object auditing
```

**Session auditing: by statement class**

| Class | Statements logged |
|---|---|
| `READ` | `SELECT`, `COPY ... TO` |
| `WRITE` | `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE`, `COPY ... FROM` |
| `FUNCTION` | Function calls and `DO` blocks |
| `ROLE` | `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, `CREATE/ALTER/DROP ROLE` |
| `DDL` | All DDL not in `ROLE` |
| `MISC` | `DISCARD`, `FETCH`, `CHECKPOINT`, `VACUUM`, `SET` |
| `ALL` | Everything |

Classes can be set per role or database, so you can audit administrators more heavily than the application:

```sql
ALTER ROLE migrator SET pgaudit.log = 'all';              -- everything a privileged role does
ALTER DATABASE shop SET pgaudit.log = 'ddl, role';        -- baseline for everyone in shop
```

**Object auditing: by table and column.** Logging every `SELECT` of a busy application would drown the log. Object auditing logs only statements that touch chosen objects, chosen by granting privileges to an "auditor" role that never logs in:

```sql
CREATE ROLE auditor NOLOGIN;
ALTER SYSTEM SET pgaudit.role = 'auditor';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

GRANT SELECT (tax_id) ON customers TO auditor;            -- log every read of the tax_id column
GRANT UPDATE, DELETE ON accounts TO auditor;              -- log every change to accounts
```

**What an entry looks like**

```text
2026-10-06 09:14:02.113 UTC [48211] kim@shop 10.0.1.25(52144) psql LOG:  AUDIT: OBJECT,3,1,READ,SELECT,TABLE,public.customers,"SELECT name, tax_id FROM customers WHERE region = 'US'",<not logged>
```

| Field | Value in the example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Audit type | `OBJECT` | `SESSION` (class-based) or `OBJECT` (via `pgaudit.role`) |
| Statement ID, substatement ID | `3`, `1` | Statement number in the session; position within it (functions, CTEs) |
| Class | `READ` | Statement class from the table above |
| Command | `SELECT` | The SQL command |
| Object type, object name | `TABLE`, `public.customers` | What was accessed |
| Statement | `"SELECT name, tax_id ..."` | Full statement text |
| Parameter | `<not logged>` | Bind parameters, if `pgaudit.log_parameter = on` |

The prefix before `AUDIT:` comes from `log_line_prefix`: timestamp, process ID, `user@database`, client address, and application name.

**Choosing an audit mechanism**

| | `log_statement` | Audit triggers | pgaudit | Logical decoding / CDC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reads | `all` only | No | Yes, selectively | No |
| DDL and role changes | Yes | Event triggers only | Yes, classified | DDL not decoded |
| Old and new row values | No | Yes | No (statement level) | Yes |
| Structured output | No | Yes (tables) | Semi-structured CSV-like log lines | Yes |
| Overhead | Low to high | Per-row trigger cost | Depends on classes | Separate process |

pgaudit and audit triggers are often used together: pgaudit for *who ran what*, triggers or CDC for *what the data looked like before and after*.

**Keeping audit logs trustworthy.** A superuser can turn pgaudit off or delete local log files, so audit logs must leave the server quickly: ship them with `syslog`, a log agent, or the cloud provider's log service to a separate system (a SIEM) where database administrators cannot modify them. Alert on high-risk events such as `ROLE` class entries, `ALTER SYSTEM`, or `pgaudit` settings changes.

**Key takeaways**

- pgaudit adds structured audit records (`AUDIT: SESSION|OBJECT,...`) to the server log, covering reads, writes, DDL, and role changes.
- Session auditing selects statement classes; set heavier auditing per role or database with `ALTER ROLE/DATABASE ... SET`.
- Object auditing (`pgaudit.role` plus grants to an auditor role) logs only access to chosen tables or columns.
- Include user, database, and client in `log_line_prefix`, and be deliberate about logging parameters that may contain sensitive data.
- Ship audit logs off the server to a system DBAs cannot alter, and alert on high-risk events.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Install pgaudit, set `pgaudit.log = 'ddl, role'`, create a table and grant a privilege, and find both entries in the server log.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Configure object auditing so that every read of `customers.tax_id` is logged, but reads of other columns are not. Verify with three queries, including one that reads `tax_id` through a view.
> 3. **(Interview)** "An auditor asks you to prove who accessed patient records last quarter. What would you need to have set up in advance?" *Hint:* Consider object-level auditing on the right tables, identifying the end user behind a shared application role (`application_name`, `SET` context), log retention, tamper resistance, and clock synchronization.

#### Secrets Management

Every component that talks to the database needs a credential: application servers, migration tools, backup jobs, monitoring agents, replicas. Those secrets have a habit of spreading to source code, configuration files, CI logs, chat messages, and laptops. Each copy is a place it can leak from and a place that must be updated during rotation. **Secrets management** is the discipline of storing credentials in one controlled place, delivering them only to what needs them, and changing them without pain.

**Analogy.** Secrets management is a key cabinet with a sign-out log, instead of spare keys taped under every desk. Each key is handed to the person who needs it, its use is recorded, and the locks can be changed without hunting down every copy.

**Anti-patterns and their fixes**

| Anti-pattern | Why it is a problem | Better |
|---|---|---|
| Password in source code or committed config | Visible to everyone with repository access, forever in git history | Secret manager, injected at deploy time |
| Password in a Dockerfile or image layer | Anyone who pulls the image can extract it | Runtime injection (mounted file or secret store) |
| Password in `PGPASSWORD` or command-line arguments | Visible to other processes (`ps`, `/proc`), and in shell history | `.pgpass` file or service file with `passfile` |
| One shared credential for all services | No accountability, rotation breaks everything | One role per service |
| Secret pasted in chat or tickets | Copies outside any control | Share a link to the secret manager entry |
| `ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD 'x'` in logged sessions | Clear text in server logs | `\password` or pre-hashed SCRAM verifiers |

**libpq's built-in mechanisms**

```bash
# ~/.pgpass  (must be mode 0600, or libpq ignores it)
# hostname:port:database:username:password
db.internal:5432:shop:report_ro:Xk3...long-random...

chmod 600 ~/.pgpass
psql "host=db.internal dbname=shop user=report_ro"        # password read from .pgpass

# A service file keeps connection details and points to a password file
# ~/.pg_service.conf
# [shop-report]
# host=db.internal
# dbname=shop
# user=report_ro
# passfile=/run/secrets/report_ro.pgpass
# sslmode=verify-full
psql "service=shop-report"
```

**Secret managers and dynamic credentials.** A secret manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault) stores secrets encrypted, controls access by identity, logs every read, and can rotate secrets automatically. The strongest pattern is **dynamic credentials**: the secret manager creates a short-lived database role on demand and drops it when the lease expires, so no long-lived password exists to leak.

```bash
# HashiCorp Vault database secrets engine (sketch)
vault write database/config/shop \
    plugin_name=postgresql-database-plugin \
    connection_url="postgresql://{{username}}:{{password}}@db.internal:5432/shop?sslmode=verify-full" \
    username="vault_admin" password="..." \
    allowed_roles="app"

vault write database/roles/app \
    db_name=shop \
    creation_statements="CREATE ROLE \"{{name}}\" LOGIN PASSWORD '{{password}}' VALID UNTIL '{{expiration}}' IN ROLE shop_write;" \
    default_ttl=1h max_ttl=24h                               # credentials expire automatically

vault read database/creds/app                                # returns a fresh user name and password
```

The `vault_admin` role needs `CREATEROLE` and `ADMIN OPTION` on `shop_write` (PostgreSQL 16+), but no data access of its own. Objects should be owned by `shop_owner`, never by the temporary roles, or they cannot be dropped cleanly when leases expire.

**Passwordless options.** Managed services can replace passwords with identity tokens: AWS RDS IAM authentication issues 15-minute tokens, Google Cloud SQL and Azure Database for PostgreSQL integrate with their identity platforms, and PostgreSQL 18 adds the `oauth` method for identity providers. Certificate authentication with short-lived certificates ([Certificate and LDAP Authentication](#certificate-and-ldap-authentication)) is another passwordless option.

**Reading secrets in an application**

```python
from pathlib import Path
import psycopg

# The platform (Kubernetes, systemd credentials, a Vault agent) mounts the secret as a file
password = Path("/run/secrets/db_password").read_text().strip()

conn = psycopg.connect(
    host="db.internal", dbname="shop", user="app_blue",
    password=password,
    sslmode="verify-full", sslrootcert="/etc/ssl/internal-ca.crt",
)
# Never log the connection string or the password; log the user name and host only
```

Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded by default; enable encryption at rest for etcd, restrict RBAC on secrets, or use an external secrets operator that syncs from a real secret manager.

**Other secrets to manage.** Database passwords are not the only secrets: TLS private keys (`server.key`), pgcrypto and backup encryption keys, replication credentials in `primary_conninfo`, PgBouncer's credential files (prefer `auth_query` so passwords are not duplicated in `userlist.txt`), and cloud credentials of backup tools.

**Key takeaways**

- Keep secrets in one controlled store, deliver them at runtime, and give each service its own credential.
- Avoid passwords in code, images, command lines, environment variables visible to other processes, and logs.
- Use `.pgpass` (mode `0600`) and service files for libpq clients; mounted secret files for applications.
- Prefer dynamic or token-based credentials (Vault, cloud IAM, OAuth, short-lived certificates) over long-lived passwords.
- Inventory all secrets around the database, including TLS keys, encryption keys, replication, and pooler credentials.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Move a password from a shell script that uses `PGPASSWORD` into a `.pgpass` file and a service file, and verify the script still works. What happens if the file mode is `0644`?
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Search a repository (for example with `git log -p | grep -i -E "password|postgres://"` or a tool such as gitleaks) for leaked database credentials. For one finding, describe the full remediation, including rotation and history cleanup.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Design credential handling for 30 microservices that each use the same PostgreSQL cluster." *Hint:* Consider per-service roles, a secret manager with dynamic or rotated credentials, how services authenticate to the secret manager, poolers, auditing of secret access, and emergency (break-glass) access.

#### Compliance Considerations

Organizations that store personal, health, or payment data are subject to laws and standards that dictate how that data is protected: the GDPR in the European Union, HIPAA for US health data, PCI DSS for payment cards, and frameworks such as SOC 2 and ISO 27001 that customers demand as evidence of good practice. These documents rarely mention PostgreSQL, but many of their requirements land on the database: access control, encryption, audit trails, retention, and the ability to delete a person's data. Knowing how to map requirements to database features, and how to produce evidence, is part of a database engineer's job. (This is technical guidance, not legal advice; compliance decisions involve your legal and security teams.)

**Analogy.** A compliance framework is like a building code: it does not tell you which bricks to buy, but it requires fire exits, alarms, and inspections, and an inspector will ask you to show them.

**The main frameworks**

| Framework | Scope | Database-relevant themes |
|---|---|---|
| GDPR (EU) | Personal data of people in the EU | Data minimization, purpose limitation, right to erasure and access, security of processing, breach notification within 72 hours, data residency for transfers |
| HIPAA (US) | Protected health information | Access control, unique user identification, audit controls, integrity, encryption (addressable), transmission security |
| PCI DSS v4.0 | Payment card data | Do not store sensitive authentication data (CVV), render card numbers unreadable, MFA for administrative access, audit logs kept 12 months, quarterly access reviews |
| SOC 2 / ISO 27001 | Organizational security controls | Access management, change management, logging and monitoring, backups, incident response, with evidence |

**Mapping requirements to PostgreSQL features**

| Requirement | PostgreSQL controls | Evidence an auditor may ask for |
|---|---|---|
| Unique, individual accounts | Personal login roles, central identity (LDAP, certificates, OAuth) | Role list, `pg_hba.conf` |
| Least privilege and periodic access review | Group roles, column grants, RLS, predefined roles | Exported grants and memberships, review sign-offs |
| Strong authentication | SCRAM, certificates, `clientcert=verify-full` for MFA-like admin access | `pg_hba_file_rules`, configuration |
| Encryption in transit | `hostssl` rules, `verify-full` clients | `pg_stat_ssl`, configuration |
| Encryption at rest | Encrypted volumes, TDE, pgcrypto | Cloud/KMS configuration, key policies |
| Audit trail | pgaudit, connection logging, shipped to SIEM | Sample logs, retention settings |
| Change management | Migrations in version control, owner role, DDL auditing | Migration history, pgaudit `DDL` entries |
| Backup and recovery | Encrypted backups, restore tests ([11.3](#113-backup-and-recovery)) | Restore test reports |
| Data minimization and retention | Partitioning by time, scheduled deletion | Retention jobs and their logs |

**Retention: dropping old data cheaply.** Retention policies are easiest to implement when tables are partitioned by time, so expired data is removed by dropping a partition instead of deleting millions of rows:

```sql
-- transfers_log: a table partitioned by month (illustrative). Keep 24 months; run monthly, e.g. with pg_cron
ALTER TABLE transfers_log DETACH PARTITION transfers_log_2024_09;
DROP TABLE transfers_log_2024_09;           -- instant, no bloat; backups expire on their own schedule
```

**Right to erasure.** Deleting one person's data touches many tables, and copies remain in backups, replicas, logs, and analytics systems. A deletion routine should be explicit, tested, and audited:

```sql
CREATE PROCEDURE erase_customer(p_id int)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
  DELETE FROM transfers WHERE from_id IN (SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE owner_customer = p_id)
                           OR to_id   IN (SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE owner_customer = p_id);
  DELETE FROM accounts  WHERE owner_customer = p_id;
  -- Where records must be kept for legal reasons (e.g. invoices), anonymize instead of deleting
  UPDATE customers
  SET name = 'erased', email = 'erased-' || id || '@invalid', phone = NULL, tax_id = NULL
  WHERE id = p_id;
  INSERT INTO erasure_log (customer_id, erased_at) VALUES (p_id, now());   -- proof without personal data
END;
$$;
```

(The `owner_customer` column and `erasure_log` table are illustrative; adapt the routine to your schema.)

For backups, the usual approaches are to let backups expire within a documented retention period, and to re-apply erasures after any restore, or to use **crypto-shredding**: encrypt each person's sensitive data with a per-person key, and delete the key to make every copy unreadable at once.

**Data residency.** Some regulations restrict where data may be stored or processed. Replicas, backups, log shipping destinations, and managed-service regions all count; check them, not only the primary.

**Making compliance continuous.** Audits go smoothly when evidence is produced automatically: scheduled exports of roles and grants, configuration snapshots under version control, pgaudit logs retained in a SIEM, and restore tests recorded as they happen. The [Security Hardening Checklist](#security-hardening-checklist) gives a baseline to measure against.

**Key takeaways**

- GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, and SOC 2/ISO 27001 translate into concrete database controls: access control, authentication, encryption, auditing, retention, and erasure.
- Map each requirement to a PostgreSQL feature and to the evidence that proves it is in place.
- Partition by time to make retention cheap; write explicit, audited erasure routines, and plan for copies in backups.
- Crypto-shredding makes data in all copies unreadable by destroying per-subject keys.
- Check data residency for replicas, backups, and logs, and automate evidence collection.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** For a table of customer data you know, classify each column (public, internal, personal, sensitive) and propose a control for each class.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write and test an `erase_customer` procedure for the sample schema that anonymizes rows that must be kept and deletes the rest, and a query that proves no personal data for that customer remains in any table.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A customer exercises their right to erasure. Their data is in the primary, two replicas, nightly backups kept for 35 days, and an analytics warehouse. Walk me through your response." *Hint:* Distinguish what replicates automatically from what does not, backup retention versus restore procedures, crypto-shredding, downstream systems, and how you document completion.

#### Security Hardening Checklist

Each topic in this chapter addresses one layer of defense. Real incidents usually exploit the gap between layers: a forgotten `trust` rule, an application role that owns its tables, a backup bucket without encryption, a minor release that was never installed. A **hardening checklist** brings the layers together so they can be reviewed systematically, at setup time and again periodically, because configurations drift.

**Analogy.** A pilot's pre-flight checklist exists not because pilots do not know their aircraft, but because skipping one item out of fifty is easy and fatal. A hardening checklist does the same for a database server.

**The checklist**

| Area | Check | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Network | `listen_addresses` limited to required interfaces; port not exposed to the internet; firewall or security groups restrict sources | [Chapter 1](#1-foundations-of-database-systems) |
| | `pg_hba.conf`: no `trust` for network rules; specific rules first; final `reject` | [pg_hba.conf Rules and Order](#pg_hbaconf-rules-and-order) |
| Encryption in transit | `ssl = on`, `hostssl` rules, `hostnossl ... reject`, `ssl_min_protocol_version` at least TLS 1.2; clients use `verify-full` | [Connection Encryption with TLS](#connection-encryption-with-tls) |
| Authentication | `scram-sha-256` everywhere; no MD5 verifiers left; superuser only via local `peer` | [Password Authentication and SCRAM](#password-authentication-and-scram) |
| | Expiry for temporary accounts; one role per person and per service | [Password Policies and Rotation](#password-policies-and-rotation) |
| Roles | Few superusers; no application role with `SUPERUSER`, `CREATEROLE`, `BYPASSRLS`, or ownership of objects | [Principle of Least Privilege](#principle-of-least-privilege) |
| | Server-file and server-program predefined roles granted to nobody, or audited like superuser | [Predefined Roles](#predefined-roles) |
| Privileges | `CONNECT`/`TEMPORARY` revoked from `PUBLIC` on databases; `CREATE` revoked on `public` schema; `EXECUTE` revoked from `PUBLIC` on sensitive functions | [Schema-Level Access Control](#schema-level-access-control) |
| | Default privileges defined for the owner role | [Default Privileges](#default-privileges) |
| | `SECURITY DEFINER` functions pin `search_path` and are not owned by superusers | [Security Definer vs. Invoker](#security-definer-vs-invoker) |
| Data access | RLS on multi-tenant tables, forced, with `WITH CHECK`; column grants or masking for sensitive columns; security-barrier views | [10.3](#103-row-and-column-security) |
| Data protection | Encrypted volumes, backups, and WAL archive; sensitive columns encrypted where required | [Encryption at Rest](#encryption-at-rest) |
| Extensions and languages | Only needed extensions installed; untrusted languages restricted to reviewed code | [Chapter 9](#9-server-side-programming) |
| Logging and auditing | `log_connections`, `log_disconnections`, informative `log_line_prefix`, pgaudit for sensitive objects, logs shipped off-host | [Auditing with pgaudit](#auditing-with-pgaudit) |
| Resource limits | `statement_timeout` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` per role; connection limits | [Principle of Least Privilege](#principle-of-least-privilege) |
| Operating system | PostgreSQL runs as an unprivileged OS user; data directory mode `0700`; key files `0600`; minimal other software on the host | [Chapter 1](#1-foundations-of-database-systems) |
| Patching | Latest minor release of a supported major version; subscribe to security announcements | [11.4](#114-upgrades-and-migration) |
| Secrets | No credentials in code, images, or logs; rotation procedure tested | [Secrets Management](#secrets-management) |
| Recovery | Encrypted backups restored and verified regularly | [11.3](#113-backup-and-recovery) |

**Automating part of the review.** Many items can be checked with SQL and run on a schedule, so drift is detected without waiting for an audit:

```sql
-- 1. Risky settings
SELECT name, setting
FROM pg_settings
WHERE (name = 'ssl'                     AND setting <> 'on')
   OR (name = 'password_encryption'     AND setting <> 'scram-sha-256')
   OR (name = 'listen_addresses'        AND setting = '*')
   OR (name IN ('log_connections', 'log_disconnections') AND setting IN ('off', ''));

-- 2. Weak pg_hba.conf rules
SELECT line_number, type, database, user_name, address, auth_method
FROM pg_hba_file_rules
WHERE auth_method IN ('trust', 'password', 'md5', 'ident')
   OR (type = 'host' AND address = '0.0.0.0' AND auth_method <> 'reject');

-- 3. Roles with powerful attributes, and MD5 verifiers (requires superuser for pg_authid)
SELECT rolname,
       rolsuper, rolcreaterole, rolbypassrls, rolreplication,
       rolpassword LIKE 'md5%' AS md5_password
FROM pg_authid
WHERE rolname !~ '^pg_'
  AND (rolsuper OR rolcreaterole OR rolbypassrls OR rolreplication OR rolpassword LIKE 'md5%');

-- 4. Definer functions without a pinned search_path
SELECT p.oid::regprocedure, pg_get_userbyid(p.proowner) AS owner
FROM pg_proc AS p
WHERE p.prosecdef
  AND p.pronamespace <> 'pg_catalog'::regnamespace
  AND NOT coalesce(array_to_string(p.proconfig, ',') LIKE '%search_path=%', false);

-- 5. PUBLIC can create in the public schema (old clusters)
SELECT has_schema_privilege('public', 'public', 'CREATE') AS public_can_create;

-- 6. Tables with RLS enabled but not forced (review whether owners should be filtered)
SELECT oid::regclass FROM pg_class WHERE relrowsecurity AND NOT relforcerowsecurity;
```

Each query should return no rows (or `false`) on a hardened server; any result is a finding to fix or to document as an accepted exception.

**External references.** The CIS PostgreSQL Benchmark provides a detailed, versioned checklist with audit and remediation steps, and is a common baseline for compliance programs. Managed services handle some items (patching, disk encryption, OS hardening) for you, but not your roles, grants, `pg_hba` equivalents, or application credentials.

**Key takeaways**

- Security failures usually come from a single gap between layers; a checklist reviews all layers systematically.
- Cover network, TLS, authentication, roles, privileges, row and column controls, encryption, extensions, logging, resource limits, OS, patching, secrets, and recovery.
- Automate checks with catalog queries (`pg_settings`, `pg_hba_file_rules`, `pg_authid`, `pg_proc`, `pg_class`) and run them on a schedule to catch drift.
- Treat every finding as either a fix or a documented exception.
- Use the CIS PostgreSQL Benchmark as an external baseline; managed services cover only part of the list.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run the six audit queries on your development cluster and explain each finding. Which ones would you accept on a laptop but not in production?
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Turn the audit queries into a script that exits with a non-zero status if any check fails, and run it in CI against a freshly provisioned database built from your infrastructure code.
> 3. **(Interview)** "You inherit a production PostgreSQL server with no documentation. What are the first ten things you check for security, and in what order?" *Hint:* Prioritize by exposure and impact: network reachability and `pg_hba.conf`, superusers and application role privileges, TLS, patch level, backups and their encryption, then logging and auditing.

<a id="11-administration-and-operations"></a>
## 11. Administration and Operations

Designing a good schema and writing fast queries matter only if the server underneath stays configured correctly, keeps data safe across crashes, can be restored after a disaster, can be upgraded without losing a weekend, and is watched by people who notice problems before users do. This chapter covers that operational side of PostgreSQL: how the server is configured, how the write-ahead log provides durability, how backups and point-in-time recovery work, how to upgrade and migrate, and the routine practices that keep a production database healthy. These are the skills that separate "it works on my machine" from "it has run for five years without losing a row".

<a id="111-server-configuration"></a>
### 11.1 Server Configuration

PostgreSQL exposes several hundred settings that control memory, connections, logging, durability, and more; this subchapter explains where those settings live, how and when changes take effect, how to scope them to a database or role, and which limits and logging settings every production server should set deliberately.

#### postgresql.conf Structure

A database server needs to know hundreds of things before it can serve a single query: how much memory to use for caching, which network interfaces to listen on, where to write logs, how aggressively to flush data to disk. Hard-coding these would make one server fit nobody, so PostgreSQL reads them from configuration. The main source is a plain text file called `postgresql.conf`, but it is only one layer of a stack of sources that are merged into the final value of each setting (each setting is also called a **parameter** or a **GUC**, short for Grand Unified Configuration, the name of the subsystem that manages them).

**Analogy.** Think of the configuration as a stack of transparent sheets laid on top of each other. The bottom sheet holds the compiled-in defaults. Each sheet above it (the config file, `ALTER SYSTEM`, the database, the role, the session) can write a new value over a spot on the sheet below. What you see from above, the effective value, is the top-most value written for each setting.

**Finding the file**

```sql
SHOW config_file;
--                config_file
-- -----------------------------------------
--  /etc/postgresql/17/main/postgresql.conf     -- Debian/Ubuntu; $PGDATA/postgresql.conf for most other installs

SHOW data_directory;
SHOW hba_file;      -- pg_hba.conf (10.1)
SHOW ident_file;    -- pg_ident.conf
```

From the shell, the server binary itself can report a value without a running server, which is handy in scripts:

```bash
postgres -D /var/lib/postgresql/17/main -C shared_buffers   # prints the value the server would use
```

**File syntax.** The file is a list of `name = value` lines. The `=` is optional, whitespace is ignored, and `#` starts a comment. The shipped file is mostly commented-out defaults grouped into sections, which serves as documentation.

```ini
# -----------------------------
# CONNECTIONS AND AUTHENTICATION
# -----------------------------
listen_addresses = '10.0.1.10, localhost'   # strings are single-quoted
port = 5432                                 # integers need no quotes
max_connections = 200

# -----------------------------
# RESOURCE USAGE
# -----------------------------
shared_buffers = 8GB                        # memory units: B, kB, MB, GB, TB (base 1024)
work_mem = 32MB
maintenance_work_mem = 1GB

# -----------------------------
# WRITE-AHEAD LOG
# -----------------------------
checkpoint_timeout = 15min                  # time units: us, ms, s, min, h, d
synchronous_commit = on                     # booleans: on/off, true/false, yes/no, 1/0
wal_compression = zstd                      # enums are unquoted words (quotes also work)

# A later line for the same parameter wins over an earlier one:
work_mem = 64MB                             # effective value is 64MB, not 32MB
```

Units matter: a parameter has a base unit (`shared_buffers` is measured in 8 kB blocks, `work_mem` in kB, `statement_timeout` in ms). A bare number is interpreted in that base unit, so `shared_buffers = 1024` means 8 MB, not 1024 MB. Always write the unit explicitly.

**The configuration stack.** For any setting, later sources override earlier ones:

```text
 highest precedence
   ^   SET LOCAL inside a transaction           (until COMMIT/ROLLBACK)
   |   SET / set_config() in the session        (until RESET or disconnect)
   |   Function-level SET clause                (while the function runs, 9.1)
   |   ALTER ROLE ... IN DATABASE ... SET        (new sessions of that role in that db)
   |   ALTER ROLE ... SET                        (new sessions of that role)
   |   ALTER DATABASE ... SET                    (new sessions in that db)
   |   Client connection options (PGOPTIONS, options= in the connection string)
   |   Command line (postgres -c name=value, pg_ctl -o)
   |   postgresql.auto.conf                      (ALTER SYSTEM)
   |   Files included from postgresql.conf       (in the order they are included)
   |   postgresql.conf
   |   Compiled-in default
 lowest precedence
```

**Inspecting the effective configuration.** The `pg_settings` view is the authoritative source. It shows the current value, its unit, where it came from, and whether it needs a restart.

```sql
SELECT name, setting, unit, source, sourcefile, sourceline, pending_restart
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('shared_buffers', 'work_mem', 'max_connections', 'log_line_prefix');
--        name       |  setting  | unit |       source       |               sourcefile                | sourceline | pending_restart
-- ------------------+-----------+------+--------------------+-----------------------------------------+------------+-----------------
--  log_line_prefix  | %m [%p]   |      | configuration file | /etc/postgresql/17/main/postgresql.conf |        533 | f
--  max_connections  | 200       |      | configuration file | /etc/postgresql/17/main/postgresql.conf |         65 | f
--  shared_buffers   | 1048576   | 8kB  | configuration file | /etc/postgresql/17/main/postgresql.conf |        131 | f   -- 1048576 x 8kB = 8GB
--  work_mem         | 65536     | kB   | configuration file | /etc/postgresql/17/main/postgresql.conf |        142 | f

-- Everything that differs from the built-in default:
SELECT name, current_setting(name) AS value, source
FROM pg_settings
WHERE source NOT IN ('default', 'override')
ORDER BY name;
```

`SHOW work_mem` and `current_setting('work_mem')` return the value already formatted with its unit, which is easier to read than the raw `setting` column.

The companion view `pg_file_settings` shows what is *written in the files*, line by line, including lines that were overridden or contain errors. It is the tool for checking a file before you reload it:

```sql
SELECT sourcefile, sourceline, name, setting, applied, error
FROM pg_file_settings
WHERE NOT applied OR error IS NOT NULL;
--                sourcefile                | sourceline |   name   | setting | applied |            error
-- -----------------------------------------+------------+----------+---------+---------+------------------------------
--  /etc/postgresql/17/main/postgresql.conf |        142 | work_mem | 32MB    | f       |                                -- overridden by a later line
--  /etc/postgresql/17/main/postgresql.conf |        210 | wal_levl | replica | f       | unrecognized configuration parameter
```

**Key takeaways**

- `postgresql.conf` holds `name = value` lines; later lines for the same parameter win, and `#` starts a comment.
- The effective value is the top of a stack: defaults, files, `ALTER SYSTEM`, command line, database, role, session, transaction.
- Always write units (`8GB`, `30s`); a bare number uses the parameter's base unit, which is often not what you expect.
- `pg_settings` shows effective values and where they came from; `pg_file_settings` shows file contents and parse errors before you reload.
- `SHOW config_file` and `postgres -C name` locate and query configuration without guessing paths.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Find your server's `postgresql.conf`, then list every parameter whose `source` in `pg_settings` is not `default`. For three of them, explain what the setting controls and why the packager or you changed it.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add the line `work_mem = 4096` (no unit) and a misspelled parameter to the file. Before reloading, use `pg_file_settings` to spot both problems. What value would `work_mem` have had if you reloaded?
> 3. **(Interview)** "A colleague changed `work_mem` in `postgresql.conf` and reloaded, but `SHOW work_mem` in the application still shows the old value. List the possible reasons." *Hint:* Walk up the configuration stack: a later duplicate line, `postgresql.auto.conf`, `ALTER ROLE`/`ALTER DATABASE` settings, a session-level `SET`, or a connection pooler keeping old sessions.

#### Configuration Contexts and Reload Behavior

Not every setting can change at any time. Some decide how much shared memory the server allocates at startup, and that memory cannot be resized while hundreds of processes are using it. Others only affect how a single query is planned and can safely differ from one session to the next. PostgreSQL records this for each parameter as its **context**, and the context tells you exactly what you must do for a change to take effect.

**Analogy.** Think of a building. Moving a load-bearing wall (`postmaster` context) requires evacuating the building, which means a restart. Changing the thermostat schedule for the whole building (`sighup`) is done centrally and every room picks it up shortly after. Adjusting the lamp on your own desk (`user`) affects only you, and you can do it whenever you like.

**The contexts**

| Context | Who can change it | How it takes effect | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| `internal` | Nobody (fixed at compile time or `initdb`) | Never changes | `block_size`, `data_checksums`, `server_version` |
| `postmaster` | Superuser, in config files or command line | Full server **restart** | `shared_buffers`, `max_connections`, `listen_addresses`, `wal_level`, `shared_preload_libraries` |
| `sighup` | Superuser, in config files | **Reload** (`pg_reload_conf()`, `pg_ctl reload`, `SIGHUP`) | `log_line_prefix`, `checkpoint_timeout`, `max_wal_size`, `autovacuum_naptime` |
| `superuser-backend` | Superuser, config or at connection start | Reload affects only **new** sessions | `log_connections`, `log_disconnections` |
| `backend` | Any user at connection start | Only **new** sessions | `ignore_system_indexes`, `jit_debugging_support` |
| `superuser` | Superuser (or a role granted `SET` on it) | Immediately with `SET`; reload for the default | `log_min_duration_statement`, `log_statement`, `session_replication_role` |
| `user` | Any user | Immediately with `SET`; reload for the default | `work_mem`, `statement_timeout`, `search_path`, `timezone` |

```sql
-- What context does a parameter have, and does it need a restart right now?
SELECT name, context, setting, pending_restart
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('shared_buffers', 'max_wal_size', 'work_mem', 'log_statement');
--       name      |  context   | setting | pending_restart
-- ----------------+------------+---------+-----------------
--  log_statement  | superuser  | none    | f
--  max_wal_size   | sighup     | 4096    | f
--  shared_buffers | postmaster | 1048576 | t     -- edited in the file, waiting for a restart
--  work_mem       | user       | 65536   | f
```

**Reloading.** A reload makes the postmaster re-read the configuration files and signal every child process to do the same. It does not drop connections, so it is safe to do at any time.

```sql
SELECT pg_reload_conf();   -- returns true if the signal was sent, not whether the file was valid
```

```bash
pg_ctl reload -D /var/lib/postgresql/17/main
sudo systemctl reload postgresql@17-main      # Debian/Ubuntu service name
```

If the file contains an invalid value, the server logs an error and keeps the previous value for that parameter. Always check the log or `pg_file_settings` after a reload. Parameters with `postmaster` context that you edited are silently ignored until restart; `pending_restart = true` is how you find them:

```sql
SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings WHERE pending_restart;
```

```text
LOG:  received SIGHUP, reloading configuration files
LOG:  parameter "shared_buffers" cannot be changed without restarting the server
LOG:  parameter "checkpoint_timeout" changed to "15min"
LOG:  configuration file "/etc/postgresql/17/main/postgresql.conf" contains errors; unaffected changes were applied
```

**Session and transaction scope.** Parameters with `user` (and, for privileged roles, `superuser`) context can be changed at runtime:

```sql
SET work_mem = '256MB';                -- for the rest of this session
SHOW work_mem;                         -- 256MB
RESET work_mem;                        -- back to the value the session started with

BEGIN;
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '5s';    -- only until COMMIT or ROLLBACK
SELECT expensive_report();
COMMIT;                                -- statement_timeout reverts automatically

SELECT set_config('search_path', 'app, public', false);  -- function form; true = transaction-local
```

`SET LOCAL` is the right tool inside connection-pooled applications (PgBouncer in transaction mode, 7.4), because a plain `SET` would leak into whichever client gets the connection next.

**Delegating parameters.** Since PostgreSQL 15, a superuser can let other roles change specific `superuser`-context parameters without making them superusers:

```sql
GRANT SET ON PARAMETER log_min_duration_statement TO support_engineer;
GRANT ALTER SYSTEM ON PARAMETER checkpoint_timeout TO ops_admin;
```

**Restart versus reload in practice**

```text
 Edit postgresql.conf
        |
        v
 Check pg_file_settings for errors ----- errors? --> fix the file
        |
        v
 SELECT pg_reload_conf();
        |
        v
 SELECT name FROM pg_settings WHERE pending_restart;
        |                         |
     (none)                    (some rows)
        |                         |
      done              schedule a restart (failover to a standby
                        first if downtime is not acceptable, 12.3)
```

**Key takeaways**

- Each parameter's `context` determines whether it needs a restart (`postmaster`), a reload (`sighup`), a new session (`backend`), or can be `SET` at runtime (`user`, `superuser`).
- A reload never drops connections; invalid values are logged and ignored, so check the log or `pg_file_settings`.
- `pending_restart` in `pg_settings` lists edits that are waiting for a restart.
- Use `SET LOCAL` for transaction-scoped changes, especially behind a transaction-mode connection pooler.
- `GRANT SET ON PARAMETER` and `GRANT ALTER SYSTEM ON PARAMETER` delegate specific settings without granting superuser.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Count how many parameters fall in each context with `SELECT context, count(*) FROM pg_settings GROUP BY context`. Pick one parameter from each of `postmaster`, `sighup`, and `user`, and describe how you would change it.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** In one session, run `BEGIN; SET LOCAL work_mem = '1GB'; SHOW work_mem; ROLLBACK; SHOW work_mem;`. Then repeat with plain `SET` and explain the difference. Why does the difference matter behind PgBouncer in transaction mode?
> 3. **(Interview)** "You changed `max_connections` and `max_wal_size` in the config file and ran `pg_reload_conf()`. What happened to each change, and how do you verify it?" *Hint:* Compare the contexts of the two parameters, then look at `pending_restart` and the server log.

#### ALTER SYSTEM and Include Files

Editing `postgresql.conf` requires shell access to the database host, a text editor, and care not to break the syntax. That is awkward when you only have a SQL connection, and it is fragile when several people or tools edit the same file. PostgreSQL offers two complementary mechanisms: `ALTER SYSTEM`, which changes server-wide settings from SQL, and **include directives**, which split the configuration into several files that different owners can manage.

**Analogy.** `postgresql.conf` is the printed company handbook. `ALTER SYSTEM` is a sticky note the administrator puts on the handbook from a remote terminal; it overrides the printed text without touching it. Include files are separate chapters (security, logging, tuning) that different teams maintain and that the handbook pulls in by reference.

**ALTER SYSTEM**

```sql
ALTER SYSTEM SET checkpoint_timeout = '15min';
ALTER SYSTEM SET log_min_duration_statement = '500ms';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();                  -- ALTER SYSTEM only writes the file; it does not apply anything

ALTER SYSTEM RESET log_min_duration_statement;   -- remove one entry from postgresql.auto.conf
ALTER SYSTEM RESET ALL;                          -- remove every entry
```

`ALTER SYSTEM` writes to `postgresql.auto.conf` in the data directory, which is read **after** `postgresql.conf` and therefore wins over it:

```text
# Do not edit this file manually!
# It will be overwritten by the ALTER SYSTEM command.
checkpoint_timeout = '15min'
log_min_duration_statement = '500ms'
```

Important rules:

- The command validates the value before writing it, so a typo is rejected instead of breaking the next restart.
- It cannot run inside a transaction block, and changes still need a reload or restart according to the parameter's context.
- It requires superuser, or `GRANT ALTER SYSTEM ON PARAMETER name` (PostgreSQL 15+).
- Never edit `postgresql.auto.conf` by hand while the server runs; the next `ALTER SYSTEM` rewrites the whole file.
- Because it overrides `postgresql.conf`, a value set with `ALTER SYSTEM` makes later edits of the same parameter in `postgresql.conf` appear to do nothing. This is the most common source of "I changed the config and nothing happened".

**Disabling ALTER SYSTEM.** When configuration is managed by Ansible, Puppet, Kubernetes operators, or Patroni, changes made from SQL drift away from the declared state. PostgreSQL 17 added `allow_alter_system = off` to reject the command. It is a guard rail for operators, not a security boundary: a superuser can still write files through other means.

**Include directives.** `postgresql.conf` can pull in other files:

```ini
# At the end of postgresql.conf
include_dir = 'conf.d'                 # every *.conf file in the directory, in file-name order
include_if_exists = 'local.conf'       # no error if the file is missing
include = '/etc/postgresql/shared/security.conf'   # error if the file is missing
```

Relative paths are resolved against the directory of the file that contains the directive. Files in an `include_dir` are processed in ASCII order of their names, so a numeric prefix gives a predictable override order:

```text
/etc/postgresql/17/main/
  postgresql.conf          # packaged defaults, rarely edited
  conf.d/
    00-memory.conf         # generated from host size by configuration management
    10-logging.conf        # owned by the observability team
    20-replication.conf    # owned by the HA tooling
    90-overrides.conf      # emergency, temporary overrides with a ticket reference
```

**Choosing a method**

| Method | Good for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Edit `postgresql.conf` | Small, single-admin servers | Merge conflicts with package upgrades, syntax mistakes |
| `include_dir` with snippets | Configuration management, multiple owners | Override order depends on file names |
| `ALTER SYSTEM` | Managed services, SQL-only access, quick changes | Silently overrides the files; can drift from version control |
| Command line `-c` | Containers, one-off tests | Hidden from anyone reading only the files |

To see which layer set a parameter, `pg_settings.sourcefile` tells you the exact file and `sourceline` the line, including `postgresql.auto.conf`:

```sql
SELECT name, setting, sourcefile, sourceline
FROM pg_settings
WHERE sourcefile LIKE '%auto.conf' OR sourcefile LIKE '%conf.d%';
```

**Key takeaways**

- `ALTER SYSTEM` validates values and writes them to `postgresql.auto.conf`, which overrides `postgresql.conf`; you still need a reload or restart.
- Never hand-edit `postgresql.auto.conf`; use `ALTER SYSTEM RESET` to remove entries.
- `include`, `include_if_exists`, and `include_dir` let you split configuration by owner; `include_dir` files apply in file-name order.
- When configuration is managed as code, set `allow_alter_system = off` (PostgreSQL 17+) to prevent drift.
- `pg_settings.sourcefile` and `sourceline` reveal which file actually set a value.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Use `ALTER SYSTEM` to set `log_min_duration_statement` to `250ms`, reload, and confirm the value with `SHOW`. Open `postgresql.auto.conf` to see what was written, then remove the entry with `ALTER SYSTEM RESET`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Create `conf.d/10-a.conf` with `work_mem = 16MB` and `conf.d/20-b.conf` with `work_mem = 32MB`, include the directory, and reload. Predict the effective value, verify it with `pg_settings`, and then add an `ALTER SYSTEM` setting to see which layer wins.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your team manages PostgreSQL with Ansible. During an incident, someone ran `ALTER SYSTEM SET max_wal_size = '50GB'`. Months later, an Ansible change to `max_wal_size` has no effect. Why, and how do you prevent it from happening again?" *Hint:* Think about the order in which the files are read, how to detect entries in `postgresql.auto.conf`, and `allow_alter_system`.

#### Per-Database and Per-Role Settings

One server often hosts very different workloads: an OLTP application that must never run a query longer than a few seconds, a reporting team whose queries sort millions of rows, and a nightly ETL job. A single server-wide value for `statement_timeout` or `work_mem` cannot suit all of them. PostgreSQL lets you attach defaults to a database, a role, or a combination of both, so each workload gets sensible settings automatically when it connects.

**Analogy.** A hotel has a default room temperature for the whole building, but VIP guests have a preferred temperature on file, and the conference wing is kept cooler. When a guest checks into a room, the most specific preference applies: this guest in this wing, then this guest anywhere, then this wing, then the building default.

**Setting defaults**

```sql
-- Database level: every session connected to the 'analytics' database
ALTER DATABASE analytics SET work_mem = '128MB';
ALTER DATABASE analytics SET default_transaction_read_only = on;

-- Role level: every session of this role, in any database
ALTER ROLE app_user SET statement_timeout = '5s';
ALTER ROLE app_user SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';
ALTER ROLE reporting SET work_mem = '256MB';

-- Role in a specific database: the most specific level
ALTER ROLE etl_job IN DATABASE warehouse SET maintenance_work_mem = '2GB';

-- Removing settings
ALTER ROLE app_user RESET statement_timeout;
ALTER DATABASE analytics RESET ALL;
```

**Precedence.** When a session starts, PostgreSQL applies these defaults on top of the server configuration, from least to most specific:

```text
 server config (postgresql.conf, ALTER SYSTEM)
        |
        v
 ALTER DATABASE analytics SET ...              applies to everyone in 'analytics'
        |
        v
 ALTER ROLE reporting SET ...                  overrides the database value for 'reporting'
        |
        v
 ALTER ROLE reporting IN DATABASE analytics SET ...   overrides both
        |
        v
 SET in the session / SET LOCAL in a transaction      the client always has the last word
```

The client can still override any `user`-context setting with `SET`. Per-role defaults are therefore defaults, not enforcement: a `statement_timeout` set on a role protects against accidents, not against a client that deliberately runs `SET statement_timeout = 0`.

**Inspecting the settings**

```sql
-- psql meta-command: list per-database and per-role settings
\drds

-- Or query the catalog directly
SELECT coalesce(r.rolname, '(all roles)')     AS role,
       coalesce(d.datname, '(all databases)') AS database,
       s.setconfig
FROM pg_db_role_setting s
LEFT JOIN pg_roles    r ON r.oid = s.setrole
LEFT JOIN pg_database d ON d.oid = s.setdatabase
ORDER BY 1, 2;
--     role     |    database     |                       setconfig
-- -------------+-----------------+-------------------------------------------------------
--  (all roles) | analytics       | {work_mem=128MB,default_transaction_read_only=on}
--  app_user    | (all databases) | {statement_timeout=5s,idle_in_transaction_session_timeout=30s}
--  etl_job     | warehouse       | {maintenance_work_mem=2GB}
--  reporting   | (all databases) | {work_mem=256MB}

-- In a live session, pg_settings.source tells you which level applied
SELECT name, setting, source FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'statement_timeout';
--        name        | setting | source
-- -------------------+---------+--------
--  statement_timeout | 5000    | user          -- 'database', 'user', 'database user', or 'session'
```

**When the settings apply.** These defaults are read only when a session starts. Existing sessions keep their values, so long-lived pooled connections may need to be recycled (for example, `RECONNECT` in the PgBouncer admin console, or restarting application pools) before a new role setting takes effect everywhere.

**Typical patterns**

| Workload | Setting | Level | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Web application | `statement_timeout = '5s'` | Role | Kill runaway queries before they pile up |
| Web application | `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s'` | Role | Release locks held by forgotten transactions |
| Reporting users | `work_mem = '256MB'` | Role | Large sorts and hashes stay in memory |
| Read-only replica database for analysts | `default_transaction_read_only = on` | Database | Guard against accidental writes |
| Migrations role | `lock_timeout = '3s'` | Role | DDL fails fast instead of queueing behind long queries |
| One noisy service | `log_min_duration_statement = '100ms'` | Role | Detailed logs for one client only (needs superuser to set) |
| Multi-tenant schemas | `search_path = 'tenant_42, public'` | Role | Each tenant role resolves its own tables first |

A function can also carry its own settings with a `SET` clause (`CREATE FUNCTION ... SET search_path = app, pg_temp`), which applies only while the function runs. This is essential for `SECURITY DEFINER` functions ([Security Definer vs. Invoker](#security-definer-vs-invoker)).

**Key takeaways**

- `ALTER DATABASE ... SET`, `ALTER ROLE ... SET`, and `ALTER ROLE ... IN DATABASE ... SET` attach defaults that apply when a session starts.
- Precedence goes from server config, to database, to role, to role-in-database, to the session itself.
- They are defaults, not limits: a client can still `SET` user-context parameters.
- Settings apply to new sessions only; recycle pooled connections after changes.
- Inspect them with `\drds` or `pg_db_role_setting`, and check `pg_settings.source` in a live session.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create roles `oltp_app` and `analyst`. Give `oltp_app` a `statement_timeout` of 2 seconds and `analyst` a `work_mem` of 128 MB. Connect as each role and verify the values with `SHOW` and `pg_settings.source`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Set `work_mem` at the database level to 64 MB, at the role level to 128 MB, and at the role-in-database level to 256 MB. Predict the value a session sees in each of three connection scenarios, then verify. Finally, show how the client can override all of them.
> 3. **(Interview)** "How would you make sure the application cannot run queries longer than 10 seconds, even if a developer adds `SET statement_timeout = 0` in code?" *Hint:* Per-role defaults are only defaults. Consider what can and cannot be enforced inside PostgreSQL, and what a pooler, a proxy, or monitoring with `pg_terminate_backend` could add.

#### Resource Limit Parameters

A database server is a shared resource: memory, CPU, connections, disk, and locks are all finite. Without limits, a single bad query can fill the disk with temporary files, one forgotten transaction can block vacuum for days, and a connection storm can exhaust memory until the operating system kills the server. Resource limit parameters set boundaries so one misbehaving client degrades only itself, not everyone.

**Analogy.** A shared kitchen has rules: a maximum number of cooks at once, a time limit per burner, a size limit per pot, and a rule that nobody may leave food on a burner unattended. None of these rules makes the food better, but together they stop one cook from ruining dinner for everyone.

**Connection limits**

```ini
max_connections = 200                  # hard ceiling on client sessions (restart required)
superuser_reserved_connections = 3     # slots kept for superusers when the server is "full"
reserved_connections = 5               # PG 16+: slots for roles granted pg_use_reserved_connections
```

```sql
ALTER ROLE app_user CONNECTION LIMIT 150;          -- per-role cap
ALTER DATABASE reporting CONNECTION LIMIT 20;      -- per-database cap
GRANT pg_use_reserved_connections TO monitoring;   -- monitoring can still log in during a storm
```

Each connection is a separate operating system process with its own memory, so `max_connections` in the thousands is almost always a mistake. Use a connection pooler to serve many clients with few server connections ([Connection Pooling with PgBouncer](#connection-pooling-with-pgbouncer)).

**Memory limits.** PostgreSQL does not have a single "maximum memory" setting. Memory use is the sum of shared memory and per-operation private memory:

| Parameter | Scope | What it limits |
|---|---|---|
| `shared_buffers` | Shared, allocated at start | Page cache shared by all processes |
| `work_mem` | Per sort or hash **operation** | Memory before spilling to temp files; one query can use it many times |
| `hash_mem_multiplier` | Multiplier of `work_mem` for hash nodes | Default 2.0 |
| `maintenance_work_mem` | Per maintenance operation | `CREATE INDEX`, `VACUUM`, `ALTER TABLE ADD FOREIGN KEY` |
| `autovacuum_work_mem` | Per autovacuum worker | Defaults to `maintenance_work_mem` (-1) |
| `temp_buffers` | Per session | Temporary tables |
| `logical_decoding_work_mem` | Per replication connection | Changes kept in memory before spilling |

A rough worst-case estimate for capacity planning:

```text
 shared_buffers                                         8 GB
 + max_connections x work_mem x ops_per_query           200 x 32 MB x 3   = 18.75 GB   (worst case, rarely reached)
 + autovacuum_max_workers x autovacuum_work_mem         3 x 1 GB          =  3 GB
 + OS page cache and other processes                    the rest
```

The worst case is pessimistic because most connections are idle and most queries use one or two memory-hungry nodes, but it shows why raising `work_mem` server-wide is dangerous. Raise it per role or per transaction instead. Detailed tuning of `shared_buffers` and `work_mem` is in [Memory Parameters work_mem and shared_buffers](#memory-parameters-work_mem-and-shared_buffers).

**Time limits**

| Parameter | Kills or cancels | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| `statement_timeout` | Any single statement running longer | `5s`–`60s` for OLTP roles; 0 (off) server-wide |
| `lock_timeout` | A statement waiting for a lock longer | `2s`–`5s` for migrations |
| `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` | A session idle inside an open transaction | `30s`–`10min` |
| `idle_session_timeout` (PG 14+) | A session idle outside a transaction | Hours, or 0; beware poolers that keep idle connections on purpose |
| `transaction_timeout` (PG 17+) | A whole transaction longer than the limit | Optional safety net for application roles |

`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` deserves special attention. A session that runs `BEGIN`, does some work, and then waits for a slow API call or a crashed client holds its locks and its snapshot. That snapshot prevents vacuum from removing dead rows in *every* table, causing bloat across the whole database (8.5).

**Disk and other limits**

```ini
temp_file_limit = 20GB             # per-process cap on temporary file space; the query fails instead of filling the disk
max_locks_per_transaction = 64     # size of the shared lock table (raise for many partitions)
max_worker_processes = 16          # all background workers, including parallel workers
max_parallel_workers = 8
max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 2
```

**A sensible baseline**

```sql
-- Server-wide safety nets that rarely hurt
ALTER SYSTEM SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10min';
ALTER SYSTEM SET temp_file_limit = '50GB';

-- Strict limits for the application role
ALTER ROLE app_user SET statement_timeout = '15s';
ALTER ROLE app_user SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';
ALTER ROLE app_user SET lock_timeout = '5s';

-- Generous limits for reporting, but bounded
ALTER ROLE reporting SET statement_timeout = '15min';
ALTER ROLE reporting SET work_mem = '256MB';

SELECT pg_reload_conf();
```

When a limit triggers, the client receives a specific error, which makes the cause easy to identify in logs and application monitoring:

```text
ERROR:  canceling statement due to statement timeout
ERROR:  canceling statement due to lock timeout
FATAL:  terminating connection due to idle-in-transaction timeout
ERROR:  temporary file size exceeds temp_file_limit (52428800kB)
FATAL:  sorry, too many clients already
FATAL:  too many connections for role "app_user"
```

**Outside PostgreSQL.** The operating system adds its own limits: systemd `LimitNOFILE` for file descriptors, cgroup memory limits in containers, and the Linux OOM killer. If the OOM killer terminates a backend, the postmaster restarts all sessions and runs crash recovery. On dedicated Linux hosts, set `vm.overcommit_memory = 2` so allocations fail with an error inside PostgreSQL instead of triggering the OOM killer.

**Key takeaways**

- Each connection is a process; keep `max_connections` modest and use a pooler. Reserve slots for superusers and monitoring.
- `work_mem` applies per operation, not per query or per server; raise it per role or per transaction, not globally.
- Time limits (`statement_timeout`, `lock_timeout`, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, `transaction_timeout`) stop runaway work and forgotten transactions.
- `temp_file_limit` turns a disk-filling query into a single failed query.
- Set strict limits on application roles and looser, still bounded, limits on reporting and maintenance roles.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Set `statement_timeout = '2s'` in a session and run `SELECT pg_sleep(5)`. Then set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5s'`, run `BEGIN;`, wait 10 seconds, and run `SELECT 1`. Record both errors.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Compute the worst-case memory estimate for a server with 64 GB RAM, `shared_buffers = 16GB`, `max_connections = 300`, and `work_mem = 64MB`. Propose new values for `max_connections`, `work_mem`, and per-role settings that keep the worst case under the available RAM, and explain the role of a pooler.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Disk usage on the database server jumped by 200 GB in ten minutes and then dropped back. What could cause this, and which setting would have limited the damage?" *Hint:* Think about where sorts and hashes spill when they exceed `work_mem`, and how `log_temp_files` and `temp_file_limit` help.

#### Logging Configuration

When something goes wrong at 3 a.m., the server log is often the only record of what happened: which query failed, who was connected, how long a checkpoint took, which process waited for a lock. A default PostgreSQL installation logs very little, and in a format that is hard to analyze. Deliberate logging configuration, done before you need it, is one of the cheapest investments in operability.

**Analogy.** Logging is a flight data recorder. You configure what it records before takeoff; after a crash, you can only analyze what was recorded. Recording too little leaves you guessing, and recording everything fills the recorder with noise and slows the plane.

**Where logs go**

```ini
logging_collector = on                    # a background process captures stderr into files (restart required)
log_destination = 'stderr'                # also: 'csvlog', 'jsonlog' (PG 15+), 'syslog', 'eventlog'; comma list allowed
log_directory = 'log'                     # relative to the data directory, or an absolute path
log_filename = 'postgresql-%Y-%m-%d_%H%M.log'   # strftime escapes
log_rotation_age = 1d                     # start a new file daily
log_rotation_size = 1GB                   # or when the file gets this big
log_truncate_on_rotation = off            # on + a cyclic file name (e.g. %a) = fixed retention without cleanup
log_file_mode = 0640                      # let a log-reading group access files
```

Debian and Ubuntu packages disable the collector and let the service write to `/var/log/postgresql/`, rotated by `logrotate`. Containers usually log to stderr and let the platform collect output. Structured formats are easier to ship to log platforms:

```json
{"timestamp":"2026-10-06 09:14:02.118 UTC","user":"app_user","dbname":"shop","pid":48211,
 "remote_host":"10.0.1.25","session_id":"6702b4a1.bc53","line_num":7,"ps":"SELECT",
 "error_severity":"ERROR","state_code":"57014","message":"canceling statement due to statement timeout",
 "statement":"SELECT * FROM orders WHERE note ILIKE '%refund%'","application_name":"checkout-api",
 "backend_type":"client backend","query_id":-512839208833012}
```

**The log line prefix.** For plain `stderr` logs, `log_line_prefix` decides what context precedes every message. The default `'%m [%p] '` (timestamp and process ID) is not enough to tell users, databases, and applications apart.

```ini
log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %q%u@%d app=%a client=%h xid=%x '
```

| Escape | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `%m` / `%t` | Timestamp with / without milliseconds |
| `%p` | Process ID |
| `%u` / `%d` | User name / database name |
| `%a` | `application_name` set by the client |
| `%h` | Client host |
| `%c` | Session ID (stable for the whole session, useful to group lines) |
| `%l` | Line number within the session |
| `%x` / `%v` | Transaction ID / virtual transaction ID |
| `%e` | SQLSTATE error code |
| `%Q` | Query ID (needs `compute_query_id`), links log lines to `pg_stat_statements` |
| `%q` | Stop here for non-session processes (checkpointer, autovacuum), which have no user or database |

Log analyzers such as pgBadger need to know the prefix you chose ([Log Analysis with pgBadger](#log-analysis-with-pgbadger)), so pick one and keep it stable.

**What to log**

| Parameter | Recommended production value | What it captures |
|---|---|---|
| `log_min_messages` | `warning` (default) | Severity threshold for server messages |
| `log_min_error_statement` | `error` (default) | Includes the failing SQL text with each error |
| `log_min_duration_statement` | `250ms`–`1s` | Every statement slower than the threshold ([Slow Query Logging](#slow-query-logging)) |
| `log_statement` | `ddl` | All DDL, a cheap audit trail of schema changes; avoid `all` in production |
| `log_connections` / `log_disconnections` | `on` | Who connected, from where, and for how long |
| `log_lock_waits` | `on` | Any lock wait longer than `deadlock_timeout` (1s) |
| `log_temp_files` | `0` or `10MB` | Queries that spill to disk |
| `log_checkpoints` | `on` (default since 15) | Checkpoint frequency and duration (11.2) |
| `log_autovacuum_min_duration` | `10min` (default) or lower | Slow or heavy autovacuum runs |
| `log_replication_commands` | `on` on primaries with replicas | Replication connections and slot commands |
| `log_timezone` | `'UTC'` | Unambiguous timestamps across servers |
| `lc_messages` | `'C'` | English messages, which log analyzers expect |

PostgreSQL 18 also accepts a list for `log_connections` (for example `'authentication,authorization'`) to choose which connection stages are logged, while `on` and `off` keep their old meaning.

**A baseline block**

```ini
# conf.d/10-logging.conf
log_destination = 'stderr,jsonlog'
logging_collector = on
log_directory = 'log'
log_filename = 'postgresql-%Y-%m-%d.log'
log_rotation_age = 1d
log_rotation_size = 0
log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %q%u@%d app=%a client=%h '
log_timezone = 'UTC'
lc_messages = 'C'

log_min_duration_statement = 500ms
log_statement = 'ddl'
log_connections = on
log_disconnections = on
log_lock_waits = on
log_temp_files = 10MB
log_checkpoints = on
log_autovacuum_min_duration = 1min
```

**Sensitive data.** Logs can contain secrets. `log_statement = 'all'`, slow query logs, and error statements may include personal data or a password in `ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD '...'`. Mitigations: set passwords with `\password` in psql (sends a hash), restrict log file permissions, avoid `log_statement = 'all'`, and use `log_parameter_max_length` and `log_parameter_max_length_on_error` to cap the size of logged bind parameters. For a proper audit trail, use pgaudit ([Auditing with pgaudit](#auditing-with-pgaudit)).

**Reading logs from SQL**

```sql
SELECT pg_current_logfile();                 -- path of the file currently being written
SELECT * FROM pg_ls_logdir() ORDER BY modification DESC LIMIT 5;   -- needs pg_monitor or superuser
```

**Key takeaways**

- Enable the logging collector (or rely on the platform's collector) with rotation, and log in UTC.
- Use a rich `log_line_prefix` (time, PID, user, database, application, client); `%q` keeps background-process lines clean.
- Log slow statements, DDL, connections, lock waits, temp files, checkpoints, and slow autovacuum runs by default.
- `jsonlog` and `csvlog` give structured logs for log platforms; set `lc_messages = 'C'` for analyzers.
- Treat logs as sensitive data: avoid `log_statement = 'all'` and protect file permissions.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Set the baseline logging block above on a development server, reload, and trigger one of each: a slow query (`pg_sleep(1)`), a DDL statement, a failed login, and a query that spills to disk (large `ORDER BY` with `work_mem = '64kB'`). Find each entry in the log.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Enable `jsonlog` alongside `stderr`. Write a short `jq` command that lists the ten most common `state_code` values in today's JSON log, and explain what three of them mean.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Production logs are 50 GB per day and nobody reads them, yet during the last incident they lacked the information you needed. How do you redesign the logging configuration?" *Hint:* Distinguish volume from value: lower `log_statement`, raise thresholds, add context to the prefix, use structured output, ship to a searchable store, and define retention.

<a id="112-write-ahead-logging"></a>
### 11.2 Write-Ahead Logging

The write-ahead log (WAL) is the mechanism behind PostgreSQL's durability, crash recovery, backups, and replication; this subchapter explains what the WAL is, how checkpoints bound it, which settings trade durability for speed, and how the server uses it to recover after a crash.

#### WAL Purpose and Structure

When a transaction commits, PostgreSQL promises that its changes survive a crash or power loss. The obvious way to keep that promise would be to write every modified data page to disk before reporting success. That would be very slow. A single `UPDATE` may touch a table page, several index pages, and a visibility map page, all in different places on disk, and each random write costs far more than a sequential one. Worse, if the power fails halfway through writing those pages, the data files are left in a state that is neither old nor new.

The **write-ahead log** solves both problems with one rule: *before a change to a data page reaches disk, a record describing that change must already be safely on disk in the log*. The log is append-only and sequential, so writing it is fast. At commit, PostgreSQL only has to flush the log up to the commit record; the modified data pages stay in memory (`shared_buffers`) and are written later, in the background, in efficient batches.

**Analogy.** An accountant does not rewrite every ledger page the moment a transaction happens. They first write a line in a bound journal: "moved 100 from account A to account B". The ledgers are brought up to date later. If the office burns down halfway through updating the ledgers, the journal (kept in a fireproof safe) is enough to redo all the work.

**What happens on an UPDATE**

```text
 Client: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1; COMMIT;

 1. Backend modifies the page in shared_buffers          (memory only, page marked "dirty")
 2. Backend creates a WAL record describing the change   (in the WAL buffers, wal_buffers)
 3. COMMIT: WAL is written and fsync'ed up to the commit record   <-- the only disk wait
 4. Client receives COMMIT
 5. Later: checkpointer / background writer write the dirty page to the data file
           (never before the WAL record that describes it is on disk)
```

**Log sequence numbers.** Every byte position in the WAL has an address called a **log sequence number (LSN)**, a 64-bit number written as two hexadecimal halves (`0/3A4F1B8`). LSNs only grow. Every data page stores the LSN of the last WAL record that modified it, which lets recovery decide whether a record still needs to be applied. LSNs also measure distances: replication lag, the amount of WAL since a checkpoint, the WAL generated by a batch job.

```sql
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();                       -- current write position, e.g. 2B/7F1A9C28

-- How much WAL does an operation generate?
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS before \gset
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1;
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), :'before')) AS wal_generated;
--  wal_generated
-- ---------------
--  142 MB
```

**Segments and file names.** The WAL is stored as a sequence of files called **segments**, 16 MB each by default (chosen at `initdb --wal-segsize`), in the `pg_wal` directory of the data directory. Each segment is made of 8 kB WAL pages that contain variable-length records. Segment file names have 24 hexadecimal digits:

```text
 000000010000002B0000007F
 \______/\______/\______/
 timeline  high 32   segment number
   (1)    bits of     within that
          the LSN     4 GB range
          (0x2B)      (0x7F)
```

```sql
SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn());     -- 000000010000002B0000007F

-- Size of pg_wal right now (needs superuser or pg_monitor)
SELECT count(*) AS segments, pg_size_pretty(sum(size)) AS total FROM pg_ls_waldir();
```

The timeline is a counter that increases every time a server is promoted or a point-in-time recovery ends, so that WAL from alternative histories never collides ([Continuous Archiving and PITR](#continuous-archiving-and-pitr)).

**What a WAL record contains.** Each record has a header (total length, transaction ID, previous record's LSN, a CRC checksum, and the **resource manager** responsible for it, such as Heap, Btree, Transaction, or XLOG) and a body with the information needed to redo the change, plus references to the blocks it touches. The `pg_waldump` tool decodes segments into readable text:

```bash
pg_waldump -p /var/lib/postgresql/17/main/pg_wal -s 2B/7F1A9C28 -n 5
```

```text
rmgr: Heap        len (rec/tot):     72/    72, tx:     918273, lsn: 2B/7F1A9C28, prev 2B/7F1A9BF0, desc: HOT_UPDATE old_xmax: 918273, old_off: 4, old_infobits: [], flags: 0x10, new_xmax: 0, new_off: 9, blkref #0: rel 1663/16384/24576 blk 17
rmgr: Btree       len (rec/tot):     64/    64, tx:     918273, lsn: 2B/7F1A9C70, prev 2B/7F1A9C28, desc: INSERT_LEAF off: 112, blkref #0: rel 1663/16384/24581 blk 3
rmgr: Transaction len (rec/tot):     34/    34, tx:     918273, lsn: 2B/7F1A9CB0, prev 2B/7F1A9C70, desc: COMMIT 2026-10-06 09:20:11.481203 UTC
```

The `pg_walinspect` extension (PostgreSQL 15+) offers similar information from SQL, and `pg_stat_wal` reports totals since the last statistics reset:

```sql
SELECT wal_records, wal_fpi, pg_size_pretty(wal_bytes) AS wal_bytes, wal_buffers_full
FROM pg_stat_wal;
```

**One log, many uses.** Because the WAL is a complete, ordered description of every change, it is reused well beyond crash recovery:

| Use | How it uses the WAL |
|---|---|
| Crash recovery | Replays records since the last checkpoint ([Crash Recovery Process](#crash-recovery-process)) |
| Point-in-time recovery | Replays archived WAL on top of a base backup up to a chosen moment (11.3) |
| Physical replication | Ships WAL to standbys, which replay it continuously (12.1) |
| Logical replication and change data capture | Decodes WAL into row-level changes (12.2) |

**Key takeaways**

- WAL rule: a change is logged, and the log flushed, before the data page itself may be written to disk.
- Commit waits only for a sequential WAL flush; data pages are written later in the background.
- LSNs are byte positions in the WAL; use `pg_current_wal_lsn()` and `pg_wal_lsn_diff()` to measure WAL volume and lag.
- WAL lives in 16 MB segment files in `pg_wal`; names encode the timeline and position.
- The same log powers crash recovery, PITR, physical replication, and logical decoding.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Record `pg_current_wal_lsn()`, insert 100,000 rows into a test table, and compute how much WAL was generated. Repeat with an `UNLOGGED` table and compare.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Use `pg_walfile_name()` to find the current segment, then run `pg_waldump` on it and identify the records produced by a single `INSERT` followed by `COMMIT`. Which resource managers appear?
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why is it faster to write every change twice (once to the WAL, once to the data file) than to write it once directly to the data file?" *Hint:* Compare sequential and random I/O, consider how many commits can share one WAL flush, and what happens to data page writes when they are deferred and batched.

#### Checkpoints and Tuning

If dirty pages were never written to the data files, the WAL would have to be kept forever and crash recovery would have to replay everything since the cluster was created. A **checkpoint** is the point at which PostgreSQL guarantees that every page modified before a certain WAL position has been written and fsynced to the data files. After a checkpoint, older WAL is no longer needed for crash recovery and can be recycled or removed, and recovery can start from the checkpoint instead of the beginning of time.

**Analogy.** Saving a long document. Between saves, your edits exist only in memory plus an undo history. Saving (the checkpoint) costs some time, but afterwards the history before the save is no longer needed to rebuild the document. Saving every second wastes time; saving once a day means a crash costs hours of replay.

**What a checkpoint does**

```text
 1. Record the current WAL insert position as the REDO point
 2. Write every dirty buffer in shared_buffers to the data files
    (spread over time, see checkpoint_completion_target)
 3. fsync the data files
 4. Write a checkpoint record to the WAL and update pg_control with its location
 5. Remove or recycle WAL segments older than the REDO point
    (unless needed by archiving, replication slots, or wal_keep_size)
```

**What triggers a checkpoint**

| Trigger | Setting | Log reason |
|---|---|---|
| Time since the last checkpoint | `checkpoint_timeout` (default `5min`) | `checkpoint starting: time` |
| WAL generated since the last checkpoint | `max_wal_size` (default `1GB`, a soft limit) | `checkpoint starting: wal` |
| Manual | `CHECKPOINT;` | `checkpoint starting: immediate force wait` |
| Shutdown, start of a base backup, `CREATE DATABASE` | n/a | `shutdown`, `force wait` |

Ideally almost all checkpoints are triggered by **time**. Checkpoints triggered by WAL volume mean `max_wal_size` is too small for the write load, so checkpoints happen more often than planned.

**Spreading the I/O.** Writing gigabytes of dirty pages at full speed would starve queries of disk bandwidth. The checkpointer paces itself to finish within `checkpoint_completion_target` (default `0.9`) of the interval, so a 15-minute checkpoint spreads its writes over about 13.5 minutes.

**The trade-off**

| Shorter interval (frequent checkpoints) | Longer interval (rare checkpoints) |
|---|---|
| Faster crash recovery (less WAL to replay) | Slower crash recovery |
| Less WAL on disk | More WAL in `pg_wal` (up to about `max_wal_size`) |
| More total writes: a hot page is written once per checkpoint | Hot pages are written less often |
| More full-page images in WAL ([Full Page Writes](#full-page-writes)) | Fewer full-page images, much less WAL |

For most write-heavy servers, the default 5 minutes is too short. Typical production values are 15 to 30 minutes, with `max_wal_size` large enough that WAL volume rarely forces a checkpoint.

```ini
checkpoint_timeout = 15min
max_wal_size = 16GB                 # soft limit; size it to cover ~1 timeout at peak write rate
min_wal_size = 2GB                  # keep this much WAL recycled instead of deleted
```
